days.title: Multi-Account Governance with AWS Organizations and Control Tower

concepts.heading: AWS Organizations and OU Design
concepts.body: AWS Organizations lets a company centrally manage many AWS accounts under one management account, grouping member accounts into Organizational Units (OUs) that mirror business units, environments, or compliance boundaries. Consolidated billing aggregates usage across every member account, so the organization reaches volume-pricing tiers that isolated accounts never would. A well-designed OU hierarchy, such as separate Security, Infrastructure, and Workloads OUs, lets policies attach at the right level instead of being managed account by account. On the exam, dozens of accounts needing centralized billing or policy control is the signal to reach for Organizations.

concepts.heading: Service Control Policies as Guardrails
concepts.body: Service Control Policies (SCPs) attach to an account or OU and define the maximum permissions available to every principal inside it, no matter what that principal's own IAM policy allows. Unlike an IAM policy, an SCP never grants permissions by itself; it can only restrict, so a principal still needs an explicit IAM allow underneath an SCP's ceiling to actually act. A frequent exam trap expects an SCP alone to grant access, but without an identity- or resource-based allow underneath it, the SCP permits nothing. SCPs are the standard way to block an entire Region, service, or action organization-wide.

concepts.heading: Control Tower Landing Zones and Account Factory
concepts.body: AWS Control Tower automates a multi-account landing zone on top of Organizations, deploying mandatory and strongly recommended guardrails (built from SCPs and Config rules) plus a centralized logging and audit account out of the box. Account Factory, its account-vending capability, provisions new accounts already configured with the organization's baseline networking, logging, and guardrails, removing manual setup for every new team. This matters most in scenarios describing frequent, standardized account creation. Control Tower is an opinionated automation layer built on Organizations and SCPs, not a replacement for either.

concepts.heading: Blast Radius and Environment Isolation
concepts.body: Splitting workloads across separate AWS accounts limits the blast radius of a security incident, misconfiguration, or cost overrun to a single account instead of the whole organization. Typical isolation boundaries include environment (production versus non-production), business unit, and regulatory scope, such as keeping PCI-scoped workloads in their own account. Account-level billing is also a hard boundary for cost allocation that does not depend on tagging discipline the way a shared account would. A scenario describing the need to contain a compromised workload's impact, or to cleanly separate billing ownership, is pointing toward multiple accounts rather than one shared account with IAM-only separation.

examPoints: A scenario asking to automatically enforce a security baseline on every newly created account describes Control Tower's Account Factory, not a manual per-account setup process.
A scenario asking to block an entire AWS Region or a specific API action across every account in an OU, regardless of any IAM allow, describes an SCP guardrail.

quiz.q: A company is expanding from 3 to over 40 AWS accounts as new product teams onboard. Leadership wants every new account to start with a standardized security baseline, centralized logging, and a consistent network setup without manual configuration. Which solution should the cloud team implement?
choices: Document a manual account setup checklist for each new team
Deploy AWS Control Tower and use Account Factory to provision new accounts
Create a single shared account and use IAM roles to separate teams
Apply AWS Config rules individually to each new account after it is created
quiz.explain: Control Tower's Account Factory automates baseline configuration for every new account; a single shared account (choice C) would eliminate the isolation and blast-radius benefits a multi-account strategy is meant to provide.

quiz.q: A security team wants to guarantee that no account in the Sandbox OU can ever launch resources outside the us-east-1 Region, even if a developer's IAM policy would otherwise allow it. What should they implement?
choices: An IAM permissions boundary on each developer's IAM role
An SCP attached to the Sandbox OU that denies actions when the request Region is not us-east-1
A CloudWatch alarm that notifies on cross-Region activity
A resource-based policy on every S3 bucket in the OU
quiz.explain: Only an SCP acts as an organization-wide guardrail that overrides any IAM allow at the account level; a permissions boundary (choice A) would have to be applied consistently to every principal and does not enforce at the OU level.

days.recap: Organizations centralizes billing and grouping via OUs, SCPs act only as permission ceilings that never grant access, and Control Tower automates landing-zone guardrails plus standardized account provisioning through Account Factory.

days.title: Choosing a VPC Connectivity Model: Peering, Transit Gateway, and PrivateLink

concepts.heading: VPC Peering and Its Limits
concepts.body: VPC Peering creates a direct, one-to-one network connection between two VPCs, letting resources in each communicate using private IP addresses as if they were on the same network. Peering connections are not transitive, meaning if VPC A peers with VPC B and VPC B peers with VPC C, traffic cannot flow from A to C through B. As the number of VPCs that need to talk to each other grows, this forces a full-mesh topology where the number of connections grows roughly with the square of the VPC count, which quickly becomes unmanageable to route and secure. Peering is best suited to a small, stable number of VPCs with simple connectivity needs.

concepts.heading: AWS Transit Gateway as a Hub
concepts.body: AWS Transit Gateway acts as a regional network transit hub, letting hundreds of VPCs and on-premises networks (via VPN or Direct Connect) connect through a single attachment instead of a mesh of peering connections. Because Transit Gateway supports transitive routing, a VPC attached to it can reach every other attached network without a direct peering relationship. Multiple route tables on the Transit Gateway allow traffic segmentation, for example keeping production and development VPCs unable to route to each other even though both attach to the same gateway. This centralization is why Transit Gateway is the standard answer for large or growing numbers of VPCs needing shared, centrally managed connectivity.

concepts.heading: AWS PrivateLink for Service-Level Access
concepts.body: AWS PrivateLink exposes a specific service, rather than an entire VPC's network, privately over the AWS backbone using interface VPC endpoints, so consumer traffic never traverses the public internet. It follows a provider-consumer model: a service provider exposes an endpoint service, and consumers create interface endpoints in their own VPCs to reach it, without any VPC peering or route table changes needed. This is the preferred pattern when only a single application or SaaS product needs to be reached privately, since it avoids exposing the entire producer VPC's address space to the consumer. PrivateLink also avoids CIDR overlap conflicts that can block VPC peering between VPCs sharing address ranges.

concepts.heading: Choosing Between the Three Models
concepts.body: The choice generally comes down to scope and scale: a handful of VPCs with simple, stable connectivity needs fit VPC Peering; dozens to hundreds of VPCs and on-premises networks needing centralized, transitive routing call for Transit Gateway; and exposing one specific service without connecting entire networks calls for PrivateLink. A common exam pattern combines these, for example using Transit Gateway for general VPC-to-VPC and on-premises routing while using PrivateLink for a shared services VPC that hosts a sensitive internal API only a subset of consumers should reach.

examPoints: A scenario describing dozens of VPCs and on-premises networks that need centralized, segmented routing points to Transit Gateway, not a mesh of individual VPC peering connections.
A scenario asking to expose one specific internal service or SaaS product privately, without connecting entire VPC networks together, points to PrivateLink rather than peering or Transit Gateway.

quiz.q: A company has 60 VPCs across several business units that all need to communicate with each other and with an on-premises data center, with the ability to isolate certain VPCs from others using routing rules. What should a solutions architect recommend?
choices: Create individual VPC peering connections between every pair of VPCs
Deploy AWS Transit Gateway with separate route tables to control which VPCs can reach each other
Use AWS PrivateLink to connect every VPC to every other VPC
Use a single VPC for all workloads to avoid inter-VPC routing
quiz.explain: Transit Gateway centralizes routing for large numbers of VPCs and supports route-table-based segmentation; a full mesh of peering connections (choice A) does not scale to 60 VPCs and cannot easily express isolation rules.

quiz.q: A SaaS company wants to let hundreds of customer VPCs privately reach a single API service it hosts, without allowing those customers any other network access into its VPC. Which approach fits best?
choices: VPC Peering with each customer VPC
AWS Transit Gateway shared across all customer accounts
AWS PrivateLink with an interface VPC endpoint exposing only the API service
A public internet-facing load balancer with IP allow-listing
quiz.explain: PrivateLink exposes only the specific service endpoint to consumers without granting broader network access; peering (choice A) would expose the entire VPC's address space instead of a single service.

days.recap: VPC Peering is one-to-one and non-transitive (a full mesh does not scale), Transit Gateway is a hub-and-spoke model supporting transitive routing and route-table segmentation, and PrivateLink privately exposes a single service without connecting whole networks.

days.title: Hybrid Network Connectivity: Direct Connect, VPN, and DX Gateway

concepts.heading: Site-to-Site VPN Characteristics
concepts.body: AWS Site-to-Site VPN establishes an IPsec tunnel over the public internet between an on-premises gateway and a VPC, and can typically be provisioned within hours. Because the traffic still rides over the public internet, both bandwidth and latency are variable and depend on general internet conditions rather than a guaranteed, dedicated path. This makes VPN a strong fit for scenarios needing fast setup, lower cost, or a backup path, but a poor fit where the workload demands consistent throughput or predictable latency. Each VPN connection also has a practical throughput ceiling per tunnel, so very high-bandwidth needs usually push toward Direct Connect instead.

concepts.heading: AWS Direct Connect for Dedicated Bandwidth
concepts.body: AWS Direct Connect establishes a dedicated, private physical network connection between an on-premises location and AWS, bypassing the public internet entirely and providing consistent bandwidth and lower, more predictable latency. The tradeoff is provisioning time: establishing a new physical cross-connect through a Direct Connect location typically takes weeks, which makes it unsuitable as a quick or temporary solution. Direct Connect is the right answer whenever a scenario emphasizes consistent, high-throughput, low-latency connectivity for a sustained hybrid architecture, such as continuous data replication or latency-sensitive applications split across on-premises and AWS.

concepts.heading: High-Availability Hybrid Connectivity Patterns
concepts.body: Because Direct Connect is a physical link, it can fail, so architectures needing both consistent performance and resilience commonly pair a primary Direct Connect connection with a Site-to-Site VPN configured as an automatic failover path. An even higher level of resilience uses two separate Direct Connect connections terminating at different Direct Connect locations, eliminating a single physical circuit or facility as a point of failure. The exam frequently frames this as needing both performance and disaster tolerance in the same requirement, which is the signal to combine Direct Connect with a VPN backup rather than choosing only one.

concepts.heading: Direct Connect Gateway for Multi-Region, Multi-VPC Access
concepts.body: A single Direct Connect connection terminates in one AWS Region by default, but Direct Connect Gateway lets that one connection reach VPCs across multiple Regions and multiple accounts through a single logical construct. This is the standard solution for a global organization that wants one on-premises connection point instead of provisioning a separate physical Direct Connect connection for every Region it operates in. Direct Connect Gateway operates at the routing layer, aggregating virtual private gateways or Transit Gateways from many VPCs so they can all be reached over the same underlying physical connection.

examPoints: A requirement for consistent, low-latency bandwidth between on-premises and AWS combined with a need for automatic failover describes pairing Direct Connect with a Site-to-Site VPN backup.
A requirement to reach VPCs in multiple AWS Regions from a single on-premises Direct Connect connection describes Direct Connect Gateway.

quiz.q: An enterprise needs consistent, low-latency bandwidth between its data center and AWS for a latency-sensitive workload, but must also tolerate the failure of its primary network path without manual intervention. What should the architecture include?
choices: AWS Direct Connect as the primary path with Site-to-Site VPN configured as an automatic backup
Two Site-to-Site VPN connections to the same VPN gateway
A single Direct Connect connection with no backup
quiz.explain: Direct Connect provides the consistent low latency the workload needs, while the VPN backup provides automatic failover; VPN alone (choice A) cannot guarantee the required consistent latency.

quiz.q: A global company has one on-premises Direct Connect connection and needs it to reach VPCs located in four different AWS Regions. What should they use?
choices: Provision a separate physical Direct Connect connection in each Region
Direct Connect Gateway to extend the single connection across Regions
VPC Peering between VPCs in each Region
AWS Transit Gateway alone, without Direct Connect
quiz.explain: Direct Connect Gateway lets a single Direct Connect connection reach VPCs across multiple Regions; provisioning separate physical connections (choice A) is unnecessary and far more costly.

days.recap: VPN is fast to set up but has variable bandwidth over the internet, Direct Connect gives dedicated consistent performance but takes weeks to provision, pairing the two gives high availability, and Direct Connect Gateway extends one connection across Regions and VPCs.

days.title: Advanced Access Control: Permission Boundaries, Cross-Account Roles, and IAM Identity Center

concepts.heading: Permission Boundaries as a Delegation Ceiling
concepts.body: A permission boundary is a managed policy attached to an IAM user or role that sets the maximum permissions that entity can ever have, regardless of what identity-based policies are later attached to it. This is the standard tool for safe delegation: a central security team can let application teams create their own IAM roles, confident that no role they create can exceed the boundary's ceiling, even by accident. A permission boundary differs from an SCP in scope: the boundary applies to a specific IAM principal, while an SCP applies to an entire account or OU regardless of which principal is acting. Without an identity-based policy granting the action, the boundary alone still grants nothing, exactly like an SCP.

concepts.heading: Cross-Account Access with AssumeRole and STS
concepts.body: Cross-account roles let a principal in one AWS account temporarily assume an IAM role defined in another account using the AWS Security Token Service (STS), receiving short-lived temporary credentials instead of a long-lived access key. This avoids ever sharing static credentials between accounts and lets the trusting account precisely scope what the external principal can do and for how long. A trust policy on the role in the target account specifies exactly which principals are allowed to assume it, and an external ID can be required to protect against the confused-deputy problem when a third party is involved. This pattern underlies most secure multi-account automation, auditing, and cross-account service access.

concepts.heading: Centralized Access with IAM Identity Center
concepts.body: AWS IAM Identity Center (formerly AWS SSO) provides a single place to manage user access across every account in an AWS Organization plus supported SaaS applications, letting users sign in once and select which account and role to operate under. It integrates with external identity providers such as Okta or Azure AD/Entra ID via SAML, so a company's existing corporate directory becomes the source of truth for who can access which AWS accounts. This is the standard answer for scenarios describing dozens of accounts needing centralized, federated user access instead of separate IAM users created in every account. Permission sets in Identity Center define what a federated user can do once they select an account, translating under the hood into IAM roles.

concepts.heading: Least Privilege and Attribute-Based Access Control
concepts.body: The least-privilege principle means granting only the permissions an identity needs to perform its task, and nothing more, reducing the impact of a compromised credential. Attribute-based access control (ABAC) implements this at scale by writing IAM policies that reference resource and principal tags rather than hardcoding resource ARNs, so a single policy can correctly scope access as new resources and teams are added without being rewritten. ABAC is particularly useful in fast-growing environments where a role-based, ARN-specific policy would require constant updates as new resources are provisioned.

examPoints: A scenario where a delegated administrator must be prevented from creating an IAM role with more permissions than a defined ceiling, even by mistake, describes a permission boundary.
A scenario needing centralized, federated single sign-on across dozens of AWS accounts through an existing corporate identity provider describes IAM Identity Center.

quiz.q: A company delegates IAM role creation to individual development teams but wants to guarantee that no role a team creates can ever be granted permissions beyond a defined ceiling, even if a team member misconfigures the policy. What should be implemented?
choices: A permission boundary attached when each role is created, capping its maximum permissions
A CloudTrail alert after the role is created
A resource-based policy on every resource the role might access
quiz.explain: A permission boundary caps what a specific role can ever do at creation time; denying role creation entirely (choice A) would prevent teams from creating any roles at all, which is not the goal.

quiz.q: A company with 50 AWS accounts wants employees to sign in once using their existing corporate Azure AD credentials and then choose which account and role to work in, without creating separate IAM users in every account. What should they deploy?
choices: IAM users replicated in every account
AWS IAM Identity Center federated with Azure AD via SAML
A single shared IAM user across all accounts
Cross-account roles with no central identity provider
quiz.explain: IAM Identity Center provides centralized, federated SSO across many accounts from an external IdP; replicating IAM users (choice A) does not scale and duplicates credential management.

days.recap: Permission boundaries cap what a specific IAM entity can ever do, SCPs cap an entire account or OU, cross-account roles use STS for temporary credentials instead of shared keys, and IAM Identity Center centralizes federated SSO across many accounts.

days.title: Encryption and Compliance Services: KMS, CloudHSM, Macie, and Config

concepts.heading: AWS KMS and Customer Managed Keys
concepts.body: AWS Key Management Service (KMS) is a managed service for creating and controlling encryption keys, with customer managed keys giving fine-grained key policies and full CloudTrail auditing of every key usage. Multi-Region keys let the same underlying key material be used to encrypt and decrypt data across multiple Regions, which is essential for cross-Region disaster recovery scenarios where a replicated encrypted object must remain decryptable in the secondary Region. KMS handles key storage and cryptographic operations behind a managed, multi-tenant hardware security module, which is the right fit for the vast majority of encryption needs on AWS. Key policies, separate from IAM policies, are the primary access control mechanism for a KMS key and must explicitly allow a principal even if their IAM policy also allows it.

concepts.heading: AWS CloudHSM for Dedicated Hardware Control
concepts.body: AWS CloudHSM provisions a single-tenant, FIPS 140-2 Level 3 validated hardware security module dedicated entirely to one customer, meaning AWS operators cannot access the key material stored inside it. This is the answer when a compliance requirement states that even the cloud provider must not be able to access encryption keys, a bar that KMS's default managed keys and even customer managed KMS keys do not clear because AWS still operates the underlying HSM fleet. CloudHSM requires the customer to manage cluster administration, high availability across HSMs, and key backup themselves, which is more operational overhead than KMS. It also supports specific cryptographic APIs (PKCS#11, JCE, CNG) needed by certain legacy applications that cannot integrate directly with the KMS API.

concepts.heading: Amazon Macie for Sensitive Data Discovery
concepts.body: Amazon Macie uses machine learning and pattern matching to automatically scan objects stored in Amazon S3 and classify sensitive data such as personally identifiable information (PII), financial data, or credentials, without requiring the objects to be manually reviewed. This is critical at scale, since manually auditing millions of objects for accidental PII exposure is impractical, and Macie produces findings that can feed into Security Hub or trigger automated remediation. Macie only inspects data already in S3; it does not scan databases, EBS volumes, or data in transit, which is a common exam distinction from broader data classification needs.

concepts.heading: AWS Config for Configuration History and Compliance
concepts.body: AWS Config continuously records the configuration state of AWS resources over time, letting an administrator see exactly how a resource's configuration has changed and when, which supports both troubleshooting and audit requirements. Config Rules, either AWS-managed or custom (via Lambda), continuously evaluate resources against a desired state and flag or, with Config Remediation, automatically fix non-compliant resources. Config differs from CloudTrail in focus: CloudTrail records who called which API and when, while Config records the resulting state of the resource and whether it complies with policy, and the two are frequently used together for compliance investigations.

examPoints: A requirement stating that even AWS must be unable to access an organization's encryption key material, as a compliance mandate, points to AWS CloudHSM rather than any KMS key type.
A requirement to automatically find personally identifiable information hidden inside millions of objects already stored in S3 points to Amazon Macie.

quiz.q: A financial services company must comply with a regulation stating that no third party, including its cloud provider, may ever have the technical ability to access its encryption key material. Which AWS service should it use to store its keys?
choices: AWS KMS with AWS managed keys
AWS KMS with customer managed keys
quiz.explain: CloudHSM provides single-tenant hardware where even AWS operators cannot access key material; both KMS key types (choices A and B) still run on HSM infrastructure operated by AWS.

quiz.q: A company stores millions of objects in S3 and needs to automatically identify which objects contain personally identifiable information without manually reviewing them. What should it use?
quiz.explain: Macie uses machine learning to automatically classify sensitive data in S3; Config and CloudTrail (choices A and C) track configuration and API activity, not the content of stored objects.

days.recap: KMS gives managed, auditable encryption keys with fine-grained key policies, CloudHSM gives single-tenant hardware that even AWS cannot access, Macie automatically finds sensitive data in S3, and Config tracks configuration history plus continuous compliance evaluation.

days.title: Disaster Recovery Strategy: RTO, RPO, and the Four DR Patterns

concepts.heading: RTO and RPO as the Foundation of DR Design
concepts.body: Recovery Time Objective (RTO) is the maximum acceptable time to restore service after a disruption, and Recovery Point Objective (RPO) is the maximum acceptable amount of data loss measured in time since the last recovery point. Every disaster recovery decision on the exam starts by identifying these two numbers in the scenario, since they directly determine which of the four DR strategies is appropriate and, by extension, how much the solution will cost. Smaller RTO and RPO values mean less downtime and less data loss, but require more standing infrastructure and more frequent replication, which drives cost up; there is no free way to shrink both toward zero.

concepts.heading: Backup and Restore, and Pilot Light
concepts.body: Backup and restore is the lowest-cost, slowest-recovery strategy: data is backed up regularly (commonly to S3 or Glacier) and infrastructure is provisioned from scratch only after a disaster is declared, yielding RTO and RPO measured in hours to days. Pilot light keeps only the most critical core components, typically a database being continuously replicated, running at minimal scale in the recovery Region at all times, while the rest of the stack (application and web tiers) stays defined as infrastructure as code but not running until needed. When disaster strikes, the pilot-light approach scales up the already-warm data tier and rapidly launches the remaining tiers, cutting RTO to tens of minutes rather than hours, at a moderate ongoing cost for the always-on data tier.

concepts.heading: Warm Standby and Multi-Site Active-Active
concepts.body: Warm standby runs a scaled-down but fully functional copy of the entire application stack in the recovery Region continuously, so recovery mainly involves scaling that environment up to full production capacity rather than launching new resources from scratch, giving faster RTO than pilot light at higher steady-state cost. Multi-site active-active runs full-scale production capacity in two or more Regions simultaneously, actively serving live traffic in all of them, which minimizes RTO and RPO to near zero at the highest cost of any strategy since nothing needs to be started or scaled after a disaster is declared. The exam typically signals multi-site active-active with phrases like near-zero downtime or near-zero data loss combined with an acceptance of higher cost.

concepts.heading: AWS Elastic Disaster Recovery and Route 53 Failover
concepts.body: AWS Elastic Disaster Recovery (DRS) continuously replicates on-premises or other-cloud servers at the block level into a staging area in AWS, enabling fast, low-RPO recovery by launching fully provisioned recovery instances only when a disaster is actually declared, avoiding the cost of running full standby infrastructure continuously. Route 53 health checks paired with a failover routing policy monitor the primary endpoint and automatically redirect DNS resolution to the secondary site when the primary becomes unhealthy, which is the DNS-level mechanism that operationalizes a chosen DR pattern's failover.

examPoints: A requirement for RTO and RPO measured in seconds or a few minutes, where cost is a secondary concern, points to multi-site active-active rather than any of the other three DR patterns.
A requirement to keep only a minimal, always-on core (often just the database) while the rest of the stack launches on demand during a disaster points to the pilot light strategy.

quiz.q: A mission-critical trading platform requires RTO and RPO of under one minute, and the business has explicitly stated cost is not the primary constraint. Which DR strategy should be used?
quiz.explain: Multi-site active-active keeps full capacity live in multiple Regions simultaneously, achieving the near-zero RTO/RPO required; pilot light (choice B) still requires scaling up other tiers, which takes longer than one minute.

quiz.q: A company wants to minimize ongoing DR costs while still being able to recover within about 30 minutes, by keeping only its database continuously replicated and defining the rest of its stack as infrastructure as code that launches on demand. Which strategy is this?
quiz.explain: Pilot light keeps just the core data tier running continuously and launches the rest on demand; warm standby (choice B) would keep the full stack running at reduced scale, which costs more than pilot light.

days.recap: RTO and RPO drive DR strategy choice; the four patterns in increasing cost and decreasing recovery time are backup and restore, pilot light, warm standby, and multi-site active-active, with DRS enabling low-RPO replication and Route 53 failover automating the DNS-level switch.

days.title: Enterprise Backup Strategy with AWS Backup Across Accounts and Regions

concepts.heading: Centralized Backup Policies with AWS Backup
concepts.body: AWS Backup provides a single, policy-driven service for backing up multiple AWS resource types, including EBS volumes, RDS and Aurora databases, DynamoDB tables, EFS file systems, and EC2 instances, replacing the need for separate, service-specific backup scripts. A backup plan defines the schedule, backup window, and lifecycle rules (such as when to transition a backup to cold storage or when to expire it) in one place, and can be applied to resources automatically via tags rather than being configured resource by resource. This centralization is what the exam is testing when a scenario describes needing consistent backup policy across many different AWS services.

concepts.heading: Cross-Region Backup for Regional Disaster Recovery
concepts.body: Copying backups to a second AWS Region protects against a disaster that affects an entire Region, since a backup that only exists in the same Region as the original resource would be lost along with it. AWS Backup supports defining a cross-Region copy as part of the backup plan itself, so every backup taken is automatically replicated to the DR Region without a separate process. This is distinct from application-level DR strategies like pilot light or warm standby; cross-Region backup protects the data itself, and is often combined with those compute-level strategies rather than used as a replacement for them.

concepts.heading: Cross-Account Backup for Ransomware and Account Compromise Protection
concepts.body: If backups are stored only in the same account as the original resources, an attacker who compromises that account, or a ransomware event that also targets backup data, could delete or encrypt the backups along with the production data. Cross-account backup copies backups into a separate, dedicated backup account with its own tightly restricted access, so that even a full compromise of the production account cannot reach the backup copies. This separation of duties is why cross-account backup, not just cross-Region backup, is the standard recommendation for ransomware resilience specifically.

concepts.heading: AWS Backup Vault Lock for Immutability
concepts.body: AWS Backup Vault Lock locks a backup vault into a write-once, read-many (WORM) state, preventing backups from being deleted or having their retention period shortened, even by an account's own root user, once the lock is applied in compliance mode. This immutability is what defends against an attacker (or malicious insider) with full account access attempting to delete backups to cover their tracks or force a ransom payment. Vault Lock is commonly paired with cross-account backup: the immutability protects against deletion, while the separate account protects against the compromised account ever reaching the vault in the first place.

examPoints: A requirement that backups survive even a full compromise or ransomware attack on the production account points to cross-account backup combined with Backup Vault Lock, not just increasing backup frequency.
A requirement to apply one consistent backup policy across EBS, RDS, DynamoDB, and EFS resources without separate per-service tooling points to AWS Backup.

quiz.q: A company was recently the target of a ransomware attack that encrypted production data and the backups stored in the same account. How should the company redesign its backup strategy to prevent this from happening again?
choices: Take backups more frequently in the same account
Copy backups to a separate, dedicated backup account and apply Backup Vault Lock in compliance mode
Store backups only in Amazon S3 Standard in the same account
Disable backup deletion permissions for the root user only
quiz.explain: A separate account plus Vault Lock in compliance mode prevents even a fully compromised production account from deleting or reaching the backups; more frequent backups in the same account (choice A) does not address the compromise vector.

quiz.q: A company runs workloads using EBS, RDS, DynamoDB, and EFS and wants one consistent, centrally managed backup policy across all of them, including a copy sent to a second Region. What should it use?
choices: Individual native snapshot features configured separately for each service
AWS Backup with a backup plan that includes a cross-Region copy rule
Amazon S3 Cross-Region Replication for all resource types
quiz.explain: AWS Backup provides one policy-driven plan across multiple resource types with built-in cross-Region copy; S3 Cross-Region Replication (choice C) only applies to S3 objects, not EBS, RDS, or DynamoDB.

days.recap: AWS Backup centrally automates backup policy across many AWS services, cross-Region backup protects against a Regional disaster, cross-account backup protects against compromise of the production account, and Vault Lock makes backups immutable even from the account's own root user.

days.title: Organization-Wide Cost Governance: Consolidated Billing and Purchasing Options

concepts.heading: Consolidated Billing and Volume Discounts
concepts.body: AWS Organizations' consolidated billing combines usage from every member account into a single bill, and for services with volume-based pricing tiers, that combined usage can qualify the whole organization for a bigger discount than any single account would reach alone. Each account's usage and cost remain individually visible in Cost Explorer even though billing is consolidated, so cost transparency per team or environment is not lost. A scenario describing many accounts each generating moderate usage of the same service, where combining that usage would unlock a steeper volume discount, is describing the benefit of consolidated billing specifically, not just multi-account structure in general.

concepts.heading: On-Demand, Reserved Instances, Savings Plans, and Spot
concepts.body: On-Demand pricing offers maximum flexibility with no commitment but the highest per-hour cost, making it appropriate for unpredictable or short-lived workloads. Reserved Instances and Savings Plans both trade a one- or three-year commitment for a significant discount versus On-Demand, with Savings Plans offering more flexibility since the commitment is to a dollar-per-hour spend rather than a specific instance family and Region. Spot Instances draw on spare EC2 capacity at discounts of up to 90% versus On-Demand, but AWS can reclaim that capacity with only a two-minute warning, so Spot is only appropriate for fault-tolerant or interruption-tolerant workloads such as batch processing or stateless horizontally scaled fleets.

concepts.heading: AWS Compute Optimizer for Rightsizing
concepts.body: AWS Compute Optimizer analyzes historical utilization metrics for EC2 instances, EBS volumes, Lambda functions, and Auto Scaling groups, then recommends more cost-effective configurations, such as a smaller instance size or a different instance family, based on actual observed usage rather than provisioned capacity. This directly targets over-provisioning, a common source of wasted spend where resources were sized for a peak that rarely or never occurs. Compute Optimizer's recommendations are advisory; a human or automated process still has to apply them, but they remove the guesswork of manually analyzing CloudWatch metrics resource by resource.

concepts.heading: Cost Visibility with Cost Explorer, Budgets, and Allocation Tags
concepts.body: Cost Explorer visualizes historical and forecasted spend with filtering and grouping, letting a team spot cost trends or anomalies, while AWS Budgets sends proactive alerts when actual or forecasted spend is on track to exceed a defined threshold, before the bill arrives. Cost allocation tags applied consistently across resources let cost be broken down by team, project, or environment even within a single consolidated bill, which is essential for chargeback or showback reporting in a multi-account or multi-team organization. Without consistent tagging discipline, this level of granular cost attribution is not possible even with consolidated billing in place.

examPoints: A scenario describing many accounts individually generating moderate usage of the same AWS service, where combining usage would reach a bigger volume discount, points to consolidated billing under AWS Organizations.
A scenario describing a workload with a confirmed, steady one- to three-year commitment points to Reserved Instances or Savings Plans rather than On-Demand or Spot.

quiz.q: An organization with 12 AWS accounts wants to combine EC2 usage across all accounts to reach a larger volume discount tier, while still being able to see each account's individual costs. What AWS Organizations feature enables this?
quiz.explain: Consolidated billing combines usage across accounts for volume pricing while keeping per-account cost visibility intact; SCPs (choice A) control permissions, not billing aggregation.

quiz.q: A company has EC2 instances that were provisioned at a fixed size a year ago but now shows consistently low CPU and memory utilization based on CloudWatch history. What should it use to get a data-driven recommendation for a more cost-effective instance size?
quiz.explain: Compute Optimizer analyzes historical utilization and recommends rightsized configurations; Cost Explorer (choice C) shows spend trends but does not generate sizing recommendations.

days.recap: Consolidated billing aggregates usage across accounts for bigger volume discounts, purchasing options range from flexible On-Demand to committed Reserved Instances and Savings Plans to interruptible Spot, Compute Optimizer recommends rightsizing from real usage data, and Cost Explorer plus Budgets plus tags give visibility and proactive alerts.

days.title: Domain 1 Review — Organizational Complexity

concepts.heading: Governance: Organizations, Control Tower, and SCPs
concepts.body: Domain 1 opens with governance at scale: AWS Organizations groups accounts into OUs and consolidates billing, Control Tower automates a landing zone with baseline guardrails and standardized account provisioning through Account Factory, and SCPs enforce organization-wide permission ceilings that never grant access on their own. When a scenario spans many accounts, first ask whether the requirement is about billing and structure (Organizations), automated baseline setup (Control Tower), or a hard permission limit (SCP), since exam distractors often swap these three roles.

concepts.heading: Connectivity: From Peering to Transit Gateway to Hybrid Links
concepts.body: Network connectivity decisions scale from VPC Peering for a small number of VPCs, to Transit Gateway for centralized, transitive routing across many VPCs and on-premises networks, to PrivateLink for exposing a single service without connecting entire networks. Hybrid connectivity layers on top with Site-to-Site VPN for fast, variable-bandwidth links, Direct Connect for dedicated, consistent bandwidth, and Direct Connect Gateway to extend one connection across Regions; the recurring exam signal is matching the number of endpoints and the performance guarantee required to the right tool.

concepts.heading: Identity, Encryption, and Compliance Controls
concepts.body: Fine-grained access control combines permission boundaries (capping a specific IAM entity), cross-account roles via STS (temporary credentials instead of shared keys), and IAM Identity Center (centralized federated SSO across accounts). Encryption and compliance layer KMS (managed, auditable keys) against CloudHSM (single-tenant hardware even AWS cannot access), with Macie automatically finding sensitive data in S3 and Config tracking configuration history and continuous compliance evaluation.

concepts.heading: Resilience: DR Strategy and Backup
concepts.body: Disaster recovery decisions hinge on RTO and RPO, which determine whether backup-and-restore, pilot light, warm standby, or multi-site active-active is appropriate, with cost rising as recovery time and data loss shrink toward zero. Backup strategy adds cross-Region copies for Regional disasters, cross-account backup for compromise and ransomware resilience, and Vault Lock for immutability, all orchestrated centrally through AWS Backup.

concepts.heading: Cost Governance Across the Organization
concepts.body: Cost control at the organizational level uses consolidated billing for volume discounts, a mix of On-Demand, Reserved Instances, Savings Plans, and Spot matched to workload predictability and interruption tolerance, Compute Optimizer for data-driven rightsizing, and Cost Explorer plus Budgets plus allocation tags for visibility and proactive alerting.

examPoints: When a Domain 1 scenario spans many accounts, first identify whether the core requirement is governance, connectivity, identity/encryption, resilience, or cost, since each maps to a distinct, non-overlapping set of services.

Watch for scenarios that mix two Domain 1 topics at once, such as a DR requirement layered with a cross-account backup requirement, since the correct answer often needs both pieces addressed together.

quiz.q: Which AWS mechanism enforces the maximum permissions allowed across every account in an entire OU, regardless of any individual IAM policy?
quiz.explain: SCPs apply organization-wide at the account or OU level; permission boundaries (choice C) apply to a specific IAM entity, not an entire account or OU.

quiz.q: A mission-critical workload requires RTO and RPO of nearly zero and cost is not the primary constraint. Which DR strategy fits best?
quiz.explain: Multi-site active-active minimizes both RTO and RPO by running full capacity live in multiple Regions simultaneously.

days.recap: Domain 1 wraps up: designing for organizational complexity means combining multi-account governance, scalable connectivity, layered identity and encryption controls, RTO/RPO-driven resilience, and organization-wide cost governance into one coherent design.

days.title: Infrastructure as Code at Scale: CloudFormation StackSets, Nested Stacks, and CDK

concepts.heading: CloudFormation StackSets for Multi-Account, Multi-Region Deployment
concepts.body: CloudFormation StackSets extend a single CloudFormation template into a deployment that can target many accounts and Regions at once, driven from one administrator account or, in newer StackSets with service-managed permissions, integrated directly with AWS Organizations to target entire OUs. This is the standard way to roll out a common baseline, such as a logging configuration or a security group standard, across an entire organization without manually deploying the same stack dozens of times. StackSets track drift and deployment status per target, so an administrator can see exactly which accounts or Regions succeeded or failed during a rollout.

concepts.heading: Nested Stacks for Modular Templates
concepts.body: Nested stacks let a CloudFormation template reference other templates as resources, so common infrastructure like a VPC, security groups, or an IAM role structure can be defined once and reused across many top-level stacks instead of being copy-pasted into every template. This modularity mirrors software engineering practices like functions or modules, making large infrastructure templates easier to maintain, test, and reason about. A nested stack's outputs can be consumed by its parent stack, allowing composition of complex architectures from smaller, independently testable building blocks.

concepts.heading: Drift Detection and Change Sets
concepts.body: Drift detection compares a CloudFormation stack's actual, currently deployed resource configuration against what the template defines, surfacing any resource that was manually modified outside of CloudFormation, such as through the console. This is important because manual changes silently desynchronize the infrastructure-as-code source of truth from reality, which can cause unexpected behavior on the next stack update or even accidental reversion of the manual change. Change sets, separately, let an operator preview exactly what a stack update would add, modify, or replace before actually applying it, reducing the risk of unexpected resource replacement or deletion during a production update.

concepts.heading: AWS CDK for Programmatic Infrastructure Definition
concepts.body: The AWS Cloud Development Kit (CDK) lets infrastructure be defined using general-purpose programming languages like TypeScript, Python, or Java instead of a static YAML or JSON template, enabling loops, conditionals, and object-oriented abstractions when defining infrastructure. Reusable patterns are packaged as Constructs, which can encapsulate best-practice configurations of multiple resources behind a simple, parameterized interface that a team can reuse across projects. Under the hood, the CDK synthesizes standard CloudFormation templates, so it still benefits from CloudFormation's rollback and drift-detection behavior, but development velocity and code reuse are much higher than hand-writing templates directly.

examPoints: A scenario needing the same baseline stack, such as a logging or security configuration, deployed identically across dozens of accounts and Regions describes CloudFormation StackSets.
A scenario asking whether a resource was manually changed outside of the infrastructure-as-code pipeline describes CloudFormation drift detection.

quiz.q: A company manages 30 AWS accounts through AWS Organizations and wants to deploy an identical CloudWatch logging baseline to every account and Region without manually running the same template repeatedly. What should it use?
choices: A single CloudFormation stack deployed manually in each account
CloudFormation StackSets with service-managed permissions targeting the Organization
AWS CDK deployed manually per account
Nested stacks within one account only
quiz.explain: StackSets with service-managed permissions can target an entire Organization's accounts and Regions from one place; manual per-account deployment (choice A) does not scale to 30 accounts.

quiz.q: An operator suspects that someone manually changed a security group rule in the console after it was originally created by CloudFormation. How can they confirm this without manually auditing every rule?
choices: Run CloudFormation drift detection on the stack
quiz.explain: Drift detection specifically compares deployed resource state against the template definition and flags manual changes; recreating the stack (choice B) is a drastic and unnecessary step just to detect the issue.

days.recap: StackSets deploy one template across many accounts and Regions, nested stacks modularize and reuse common templates, drift detection finds manual out-of-band changes, and CDK defines infrastructure in a programming language that still synthesizes to CloudFormation underneath.

days.title: CI/CD Pipelines and Deployment Strategies

concepts.heading: Building a Pipeline with CodePipeline, CodeBuild, and CodeDeploy
concepts.body: AWS CodePipeline orchestrates the end-to-end release process, moving an application through source, build, test, and deployment stages automatically whenever new code is committed, while CodeBuild compiles code, runs unit tests, and produces build artifacts inside managed, ephemeral build environments. CodeDeploy then handles the actual deployment of those artifacts to EC2 instances, on-premises servers, Lambda functions, or ECS services, and is where the specific deployment strategy (in-place, blue/green, canary) is configured. Together these three services replace manual, error-prone deployment steps with a repeatable, auditable pipeline that can gate promotion to production behind automated tests or manual approval steps.

concepts.heading: Blue/Green Deployments for Instant Rollback
concepts.body: A blue/green deployment stands up a completely separate, fully scaled environment (green) running the new version alongside the existing environment (blue) running the current version, then cuts traffic over to green once it has been validated. If a problem is discovered after cutover, traffic can be routed back to the still-running blue environment almost instantly, since it was never torn down, giving effectively zero-downtime rollback. The tradeoff is cost and complexity: because both environments run at full scale simultaneously during the transition, this approach temporarily doubles the compute footprint needed.

concepts.heading: Canary Deployments for Gradual, Monitored Rollout
concepts.body: A canary deployment shifts a small percentage of production traffic to the new version first, monitors error rates and performance metrics closely, and only proceeds to shift more traffic once the canary portion proves healthy, limiting the blast radius of any newly introduced bug to a small slice of users. This is the deployment strategy of choice when a scenario emphasizes minimizing the impact of a potential bad deployment through gradual, metric-driven exposure rather than an instant full cutover. CodeDeploy supports predefined canary configurations, such as shifting 10% of traffic and waiting a defined interval before shifting the rest.

concepts.heading: Rolling Deployments for Resource Efficiency
concepts.body: A rolling deployment updates instances in a fleet a batch at a time, taking each batch out of service, deploying the new version, and returning it to service before moving to the next batch, which avoids the doubled infrastructure cost of blue/green since no separate parallel environment is required. The tradeoff is that during the rollout window, both old and new versions are simultaneously serving traffic, which requires the application to tolerate running mixed versions safely, and rollback is slower since the previous version's instances have already been replaced in completed batches.

examPoints: A requirement for the ability to roll back a bad deployment nearly instantly, with cost being a secondary concern, describes a blue/green deployment strategy.
A requirement to expose new functionality gradually to a small percentage of users first while closely monitoring for errors before a full rollout describes a canary deployment.

quiz.q: A team needs the ability to instantly roll back to the previous version if a deployment causes errors, and is willing to accept temporarily running double the infrastructure during each release. Which deployment strategy should they use?
quiz.explain: Blue/green keeps the old environment fully running until cutover is confirmed, enabling instant rollback; a rolling deployment (choice A) has already replaced old instances by the time an issue might be discovered.

quiz.q: A team wants to release a new feature to only 10% of production traffic first, closely watch error rates, and then gradually increase exposure. Which deployment strategy fits this requirement?
quiz.explain: Canary deployments are specifically designed for gradual, metric-monitored traffic shifting; blue/green (choice B) typically cuts over all traffic at once after validation, not incrementally.

days.recap: CodePipeline orchestrates source-to-deploy automation with CodeBuild handling builds and CodeDeploy handling releases; blue/green enables instant rollback at double cost, canary shifts traffic gradually while monitoring, and rolling deployments are cost-efficient but slower to roll back.

days.title: Designing for Business Continuity: Route 53 Routing and Global Accelerator

concepts.heading: Designing DR Into New Architectures From Day One
concepts.body: Because a brand-new application has no existing infrastructure constraints, its DR strategy (pilot light, warm standby, or multi-site active-active, based on the same RTO/RPO analysis used for existing systems) can be designed into the architecture from the start rather than retrofitted later. This often makes multi-Region patterns cheaper and simpler to implement for new solutions than for legacy ones, since the application can be built to be Region-agnostic and stateless from the beginning, avoiding the refactoring effort a legacy system would need to reach the same resilience.

concepts.heading: Route 53 Routing Policies
concepts.body: Route 53 supports several routing policies suited to different needs: failover routing automatically shifts traffic to a secondary resource when the primary fails a health check; weighted routing shifts a configurable percentage of traffic to different resources, useful for gradual DNS-level rollouts; latency-based routing sends users to the Region that provides the lowest measured latency; and geolocation routing routes based on the geographic location of the requester, useful for data residency or content localization requirements. Choosing the right policy depends on whether the goal is failover, gradual rollout, performance, or geographic compliance.

concepts.heading: Route 53 Health Checks
concepts.body: Route 53 health checks periodically probe an endpoint's health via HTTP, HTTPS, or TCP, and can also be based on a CloudWatch alarm, and their result drives failover and weighted routing decisions automatically without manual intervention. Health checks can be configured with a threshold of consecutive failures before an endpoint is marked unhealthy, balancing rapid failover detection against avoiding false positives from a single transient blip.

concepts.heading: AWS Global Accelerator for Faster, More Reliable Failover
concepts.body: AWS Global Accelerator provisions static anycast IP addresses that route user traffic to the nearest AWS edge location, then carries that traffic over the AWS global backbone network to the application, which both reduces latency and improves reliability versus the public internet path. Because Global Accelerator's failover happens at the network layer rather than through DNS resolution, it avoids the delay caused by DNS caching and time-to-live (TTL) propagation that can slow down a Route 53-only failover, since clients keep using the same static IP addresses even after the backend Region changes. This makes Global Accelerator the preferred choice when a scenario specifically calls out eliminating DNS propagation delay during failover.

examPoints: A requirement to fail over between Regions without waiting for DNS TTL propagation delay describes AWS Global Accelerator rather than Route 53 failover routing alone.
A requirement to gradually shift a small percentage of traffic to a new version at the DNS level describes Route 53 weighted routing.

quiz.q: A newly designed global application must fail over to a secondary Region within seconds of a Regional outage, without being slowed down by DNS TTL propagation delays across client resolvers. What should the architecture use?
choices: AWS Global Accelerator with static anycast IP addresses
A hard-coded IP address in client applications
quiz.explain: Global Accelerator fails over at the network layer using static anycast IPs, avoiding DNS propagation delay; Route 53 simple routing (choice A) has no failover capability at all.

quiz.q: A team wants to expose a new feature to exactly 5% of production traffic at the DNS level and gradually increase that percentage over time. Which Route 53 routing policy should they use?
quiz.explain: Weighted routing lets traffic be split by percentage across resources; failover routing (choice A) is binary (primary or secondary), not percentage-based.

days.recap: New solutions can design DR in from the start; Route 53 offers failover, weighted, latency-based, and geolocation routing policies driven by health checks, while Global Accelerator provides faster, DNS-independent failover using static anycast IPs over the AWS backbone.

days.title: Securing New Applications: WAF, Shield, and Secrets Manager

concepts.heading: AWS WAF for Layer 7 Protection
concepts.body: AWS WAF is a web application firewall that inspects HTTP/HTTPS requests at layer 7 and blocks common web exploits such as SQL injection and cross-site scripting, using either AWS-managed rule groups covering common threat patterns or custom rules tailored to the application. Rate-based rules track the request rate from individual IP addresses and automatically block sources that exceed a defined threshold, which is effective against application-layer flooding and scraping bots that a network-layer control cannot see. WAF attaches to CloudFront, an Application Load Balancer, API Gateway, or AWS AppSync, and its rules can be shared across resources using AWS Firewall Manager in a multi-account setup.

concepts.heading: AWS Shield Standard vs. Shield Advanced
concepts.body: AWS Shield Standard is automatically enabled at no additional cost for every AWS customer and defends against common, frequently occurring layer 3/4 network and transport-layer DDoS attacks. AWS Shield Advanced is a paid service that adds detection and mitigation for larger and more sophisticated attacks, near-real-time visibility into attacks, integration with WAF for automatic rule creation during an attack, access to the AWS DDoS Response Team (DRT) for hands-on assistance, and cost protection that credits scaling charges incurred as a direct result of a DDoS attack. Shield Advanced is the answer whenever a scenario specifically calls for guaranteed cost protection or dedicated expert support during an attack, not just baseline mitigation.

concepts.heading: AWS Secrets Manager for Automated Credential Rotation
concepts.body: AWS Secrets Manager stores sensitive values like database credentials encrypted at rest, and its distinguishing capability is native, automated rotation, which can invoke a Lambda function on a schedule to change the credential both in the secret store and in the underlying database (for supported engines like RDS) without any application downtime. This removes hardcoded credentials from application code and configuration files entirely, since the application instead calls the Secrets Manager API at runtime to retrieve the current value. Automated rotation is the key differentiator the exam tests for, since it is the feature that makes Secrets Manager the right choice over a plain encrypted parameter store when a secret needs to change on a schedule.

concepts.heading: Secrets Manager vs. Systems Manager Parameter Store
concepts.body: Systems Manager Parameter Store can also store secrets as SecureString parameters encrypted with KMS, and it costs less than Secrets Manager, but its native rotation capability is far more limited and typically requires custom automation to replicate what Secrets Manager does out of the box. The practical rule of thumb is to use Parameter Store for configuration values and secrets that rarely or never need to rotate, and to use Secrets Manager for credentials like database passwords that require regular, automated rotation as a security best practice.

examPoints: A requirement to automatically rotate database credentials on a schedule without any application downtime, and without hardcoding secrets in application code, describes AWS Secrets Manager.
A requirement to block SQL injection attempts and rate-limit abusive bot traffic at the application layer describes AWS WAF with managed rule groups and rate-based rules.

quiz.q: A new application needs its RDS database credentials rotated automatically every 30 days without any manual intervention or application downtime, and the credentials must never be hardcoded in application code. What should be used?
choices: Environment variables set at deployment time
AWS Secrets Manager with automatic rotation enabled
Systems Manager Parameter Store SecureString with no rotation
Hardcoded values in a configuration file encrypted with KMS
quiz.explain: Secrets Manager provides native, scheduled automatic rotation integrated with supported database engines; Parameter Store without added automation (choice C) does not provide this rotation capability out of the box.

quiz.q: An application is experiencing SQL injection attempts and abusive bot traffic that a network firewall cannot detect because the traffic looks legitimate at the network layer. What should be deployed?
choices: AWS WAF with managed rule groups and rate-based rules
quiz.explain: WAF operates at layer 7 and can inspect request content for SQL injection patterns and rate-limit abusive clients; security groups and NACLs (choices A and C) operate at the network layer and cannot inspect HTTP payloads.

days.recap: WAF blocks layer 7 web exploits and rate-limits abusive traffic, Shield Standard is automatic baseline DDoS protection while Shield Advanced adds cost protection and expert support, and Secrets Manager provides automated credential rotation that Parameter Store does not natively match.

days.title: Resilient Storage for New Workloads: S3 Replication, EFS, and FSx

concepts.heading: S3 Cross-Region Replication
concepts.body: S3 Cross-Region Replication (CRR) automatically and asynchronously copies objects from a bucket in one Region to a bucket in another Region, which supports disaster recovery against a Regional outage, meets data residency or compliance requirements calling for a copy in a specific geography, and can reduce latency by serving a nearby Regional copy to geographically distributed users. Because replication is asynchronous, there is a small replication lag, so CRR does not guarantee zero data loss if the source Region fails immediately after a write; it is typically paired with versioning to protect against accidental overwrites and deletions during that window.

concepts.heading: S3 Same-Region Replication
concepts.body: Same-Region Replication (SRR) copies objects to a different bucket within the same Region, which is useful for aggregating logs from multiple buckets into one for analysis, keeping a synchronized copy between production and test accounts, or satisfying a data sovereignty requirement that a copy remain within the same Region even though it also needs to live in a separate bucket or account. The exam differentiates CRR and SRR primarily by their goal: CRR is about surviving a Regional failure or serving distant users, while SRR is about aggregation, account-to-account sync, or in-Region data sovereignty.

concepts.heading: Amazon EFS for Shared, Elastic File Storage
concepts.body: Amazon EFS is a fully managed NFS file system that can be mounted simultaneously by many EC2 instances, containers, and even Lambda functions across multiple Availability Zones, automatically growing and shrinking as data is added or removed without any capacity to provision up front. This makes EFS the right fit whenever multiple compute resources need to read and write the same files concurrently, such as shared content directories for a web application fleet, which EBS cannot support since an EBS volume attaches to only one instance at a time (outside of Multi-Attach's narrower use case).

concepts.heading: Amazon FSx for Specialized File System Needs
concepts.body: Amazon FSx provides fully managed file systems optimized for specific workloads rather than EFS's general-purpose NFS model: FSx for Windows File Server offers native SMB support and Active Directory integration for Windows-based applications, while FSx for Lustre provides a high-performance, parallel file system tuned for high-performance computing and machine learning training workloads that need extremely high throughput and low-latency access to large datasets, often backed directly by data in S3. Choosing between EFS and FSx variants comes down to the protocol (NFS vs. SMB) and performance profile (general purpose vs. HPC-grade) the workload requires.

examPoints: A requirement for many EC2 instances and containers to concurrently read and write the same files, with automatic capacity scaling, describes Amazon EFS rather than EBS.
A requirement for extremely high-throughput, low-latency parallel file access for machine learning training, often reading data directly from S3, describes FSx for Lustre.

quiz.q: A new containerized application needs a shared file system that multiple containers across several Availability Zones can mount and write to concurrently, with storage capacity that grows automatically. Which storage should be used?
quiz.explain: EFS is a fully managed, elastic NFS file system built for concurrent multi-AZ access; EBS Multi-Attach (choice A) has significant limitations and is designed for a narrower clustered-application use case, not general shared file access.

quiz.q: A machine learning team needs a high-performance parallel file system that reads training data directly from S3 with very high throughput and low latency. Which AWS storage service fits best?
quiz.explain: FSx for Lustre is purpose-built for high-performance computing and ML workloads with S3 integration; EFS (choice A) is general-purpose and not optimized for this level of throughput.

days.recap: S3 CRR protects against Regional failure and serves distant users, S3 SRR aggregates or synchronizes within a Region, EFS gives elastic shared NFS storage across many compute resources, and FSx offers protocol- and workload-specific managed file systems (Windows/SMB or Lustre/HPC).

days.title: Elastic Compute Design: Auto Scaling, Load Balancing, and Fargate

concepts.heading: EC2 Auto Scaling Group Scaling Types
concepts.body: An EC2 Auto Scaling group automatically adjusts the number of running instances across multiple Availability Zones to match demand, using several scaling mechanisms: dynamic scaling reacts to real-time CloudWatch metrics such as CPU utilization or request count, predictive scaling analyzes historical load patterns (like a recurring Monday morning spike) to provision capacity proactively before the spike occurs, and scheduled scaling adjusts capacity at specific known times, such as before a predictable batch job. Choosing predictive over dynamic scaling is the right call whenever a scenario describes a known, recurring traffic pattern that benefits from being anticipated rather than reacted to after the fact.

concepts.heading: Choosing the Right Load Balancer Type
concepts.body: The Application Load Balancer (ALB) operates at layer 7 and can route based on URL path, hostname, or HTTP headers, making it the standard choice for microservices architectures that need to direct different paths to different backend services. The Network Load Balancer (NLB) operates at layer 4, handling millions of requests per second with ultra-low latency and supporting static IP addresses, which fits use cases needing extreme performance or a fixed IP for allow-listing. The Gateway Load Balancer (GWLB) is used to insert third-party virtual appliances, such as firewalls or intrusion detection systems, transparently into the traffic path for inspection.

concepts.heading: EC2 Auto Recovery vs. Auto Scaling Health Checks
concepts.body: EC2 Auto Recovery automatically recovers a single instance in place when a system status check fails, for example due to an underlying hardware or hypervisor issue, without changing the instance's ID, private IP, or attached EBS volumes, which is useful for workloads that are not part of an Auto Scaling group but still need automatic resilience. This is a distinct mechanism from an Auto Scaling group's own health checks, which instead terminate an unhealthy instance and launch a brand-new replacement instance as part of maintaining the group's desired capacity.

concepts.heading: AWS Fargate for Serverless Containers
concepts.body: AWS Fargate runs containers on ECS or EKS without requiring any EC2 instances to be provisioned, patched, or scaled by the customer, since AWS manages the underlying compute infrastructure entirely. This removes an entire category of operational burden, instance patching and capacity planning, while still giving the resilience benefits of running containerized, horizontally scalable workloads. Fargate is the right fit whenever a scenario wants container-based resilience without the operational overhead of managing an EC2 fleet underneath ECS or EKS.

examPoints: A scenario describing a known, recurring traffic spike that should be anticipated ahead of time rather than reacted to describes predictive scaling, not dynamic scaling.
A scenario describing a microservices architecture needing path-based or host-based routing to different backend services describes an Application Load Balancer.

quiz.q: An e-commerce platform sees a predictable traffic spike every Monday at 9am tied to a weekly sale announcement. Which Auto Scaling approach lets it provision extra capacity before the spike occurs rather than reacting to it?
choices: Dynamic scaling based on CPU utilization
Predictive scaling based on historical patterns
No scaling; keep maximum capacity always running
quiz.explain: Predictive scaling uses historical load patterns to provision ahead of a known recurring spike; dynamic scaling (choice A) would only react once the CPU metric already reflects the spike, causing a lag.

quiz.q: A microservices application needs incoming requests routed to different backend services based on the URL path (e.g., /orders vs. /users). Which load balancer should be used?
quiz.explain: The ALB operates at layer 7 and supports path-based routing; the NLB (choice A) operates at layer 4 and cannot inspect HTTP paths.

days.recap: Auto Scaling groups can scale dynamically, predictively, or on a schedule across multiple AZs; ALB (L7 path/host routing), NLB (L4 high performance/static IP), and GWLB (appliance insertion) serve different needs; EC2 Auto Recovery fixes a single unhealthy instance in place while ASG health checks replace it; and Fargate removes EC2 management entirely for containers.

days.title: Choosing a Resilient Database: Aurora Global Database vs. DynamoDB Global Tables

concepts.heading: Aurora Global Database
concepts.body: Aurora Global Database replicates an Aurora cluster from a single primary Region to up to five secondary Regions with typical replication lag under one second, using dedicated, purpose-built replication infrastructure separate from standard read replica replication. In a Regional disaster, a secondary Region can be manually or automatically promoted to become the new primary, typically within about one minute, which is dramatically faster than rebuilding a database from backups in a new Region. Secondary Regions serve low-latency local reads but cannot accept writes until promoted, which is a key distinction from DynamoDB Global Tables.

concepts.heading: DynamoDB Global Tables
concepts.body: DynamoDB Global Tables provide fully managed, multi-active (multi-master) replication across multiple Regions, meaning every Region in the global table can accept both reads and writes simultaneously, with changes propagated to all other Regions automatically. This gives every Region full read/write availability without any promotion step during a failure, at the cost of eventual consistency, since a write in one Region takes a short time to propagate to the others, meaning a rapid read immediately after a write in a different Region might not yet reflect that write. This model fits applications with globally distributed users all needing local low-latency writes, not just reads.

concepts.heading: RDS Multi-AZ vs. Read Replicas
concepts.body: RDS (and Aurora) Multi-AZ deployments maintain a synchronous standby copy of the database in a different Availability Zone purely for high availability and automatic failover; the standby cannot serve read traffic and exists solely as a hot spare. Read replicas, in contrast, are asynchronous copies specifically intended to scale read throughput by offloading read queries away from the primary instance, and a database can have multiple read replicas, unlike the single standby in a Multi-AZ deployment. Confusing these two is a very common exam trap: Multi-AZ is for availability, not read scaling, and read replicas are for read scaling, not synchronous durability guarantees.

concepts.heading: Choosing Relational vs. NoSQL for New Solutions
concepts.body: Relational databases like RDS and Aurora fit workloads needing complex joins, multi-table transactions, and strong relational integrity, while DynamoDB fits workloads needing virtually unlimited horizontal scalability and single-digit-millisecond latency on simple key-based access patterns, at the cost of needing the access patterns designed up front since DynamoDB does not support arbitrary ad hoc joins. A new solution's data access pattern, more than raw scale alone, is usually the deciding factor the exam expects a candidate to reason through.

examPoints: A requirement for a relational database that can be promoted from a secondary Region to primary within about a minute after a Regional failure describes Aurora Global Database.
A requirement for a NoSQL database accepting local, low-latency reads and writes simultaneously in every Region describes DynamoDB Global Tables, not Aurora Global Database.

quiz.q: A relational application needs the ability to promote a secondary Region to become the new primary within about a minute if the primary Region fails, while normally serving local low-latency reads from up to five secondary Regions. Which database setup fits?
choices: A single-Region RDS instance with manual snapshots
quiz.explain: Aurora Global Database is purpose-built for this cross-Region promotion pattern with sub-minute RTO; RDS Multi-AZ (choice A) only provides same-Region failover, not cross-Region promotion to secondary Regions.

quiz.q: A globally distributed application needs a NoSQL database where users in every Region can perform low-latency writes locally, with those writes propagating to all other Regions automatically. What should be used?
quiz.explain: DynamoDB Global Tables support multi-active writes in every Region simultaneously; Aurora Global Database (choice A) only accepts writes in its single primary Region until a secondary is explicitly promoted.

days.recap: Aurora Global Database gives one write Region with up to five low-latency read Regions and sub-minute promotion, DynamoDB Global Tables give multi-active read/write in every Region with eventual consistency, and Multi-AZ (availability, no read scaling) is a distinct concept from read replicas (read scaling, asynchronous).

days.title: Caching Strategies: CloudFront, ElastiCache, and DAX

concepts.heading: Amazon CloudFront as a Global CDN
concepts.body: Amazon CloudFront caches both static and dynamic content at edge locations distributed globally, reducing latency by serving content from a location physically closer to the requesting user rather than from the origin every time. Origin Shield adds an additional caching layer between CloudFront's edge locations and the origin, consolidating requests from many edge locations into fewer origin requests and further reducing origin load during traffic spikes or cache misses. Lambda@Edge and CloudFront Functions let custom logic run at the edge itself, such as header manipulation or authentication checks, without a round trip to the origin for every request.

concepts.heading: ElastiCache for Redis vs. Memcached
concepts.body: ElastiCache for Redis supports replication, clustering, and data persistence, along with richer data structures like sorted sets, hashes, and pub/sub messaging, making it suitable for session stores, leaderboards, and use cases needing automatic failover. ElastiCache for Memcached is simpler, purely a multi-threaded in-memory cache with automatic partitioning across nodes but no built-in replication or persistence, making it a good fit for simple, easily rebuildable caching of database query results where losing the cache is not a serious problem. The choice largely comes down to whether replication, persistence, and richer data structures are required (Redis) or a simple, high-throughput ephemeral cache is enough (Memcached).

concepts.heading: DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX) for Microsecond Reads
concepts.body: DAX is an in-memory cache purpose-built specifically for DynamoDB, sitting in front of DynamoDB tables and reducing read latency from single-digit milliseconds down to microseconds for cached reads. Because DAX is API-compatible with the DynamoDB SDK, integrating it typically requires only pointing the client at the DAX cluster endpoint instead of DynamoDB directly, minimizing application code changes. DAX is specifically scoped to DynamoDB and cannot be used as a general-purpose cache in front of other databases, which is the key distinction from ElastiCache in exam scenarios.

concepts.heading: Matching the Caching Layer to the Use Case
concepts.body: The right caching layer depends on what is being cached and for whom: CloudFront for globally distributed static or dynamic web content, ElastiCache for general-purpose application or database query caching (with Redis versus Memcached depending on the need for replication and richer data structures), and DAX specifically when the workload's read bottleneck is DynamoDB itself and near-zero code change is desired.

examPoints: A requirement to reduce DynamoDB read latency to microseconds with minimal application code changes describes DAX, which is DynamoDB-specific and API-compatible with the DynamoDB SDK.
A requirement for a session store shared across many web servers with replication and automatic failover describes ElastiCache for Redis rather than Memcached.
