quiz.q: An application's DynamoDB read latency needs to drop from single-digit milliseconds to microseconds, and the team wants to avoid significant changes to existing application code. What should they use?
quiz.explain: DAX is purpose-built for DynamoDB and is API-compatible with the DynamoDB SDK, minimizing code changes; ElastiCache (choice A) would require the application to manage a separate general-purpose cache layer and its own cache invalidation logic.

quiz.q: Several web servers need to share session data with replication and automatic failover in case a cache node fails. Which caching solution should be used?
quiz.explain: Redis supports replication and automatic failover, unlike Memcached (choice B), which has no built-in replication.

days.recap: CloudFront caches content globally at the edge, ElastiCache Redis offers replication and richer data structures while Memcached offers simple multi-threaded caching, and DAX is a DynamoDB-specific microsecond-latency cache requiring minimal code change.

days.title: Cost-Optimized Architecture for New Workloads: Data Transfer, S3 Classes, and Graviton

concepts.heading: Data Transfer Cost Awareness
concepts.body: Data transfer between Availability Zones within the same Region still incurs a per-GB charge in each direction, so architectures that are indifferent to which AZ a resource lands in can sometimes reduce cost slightly by co-locating chatty components in the same AZ, though this must be weighed against the resilience benefit of spreading across AZs. Traffic that would otherwise route through a NAT Gateway to reach AWS services like S3 or DynamoDB can instead use a VPC Gateway Endpoint, which is free and keeps that traffic off the NAT Gateway entirely, both reducing cost and removing a potential bottleneck.

concepts.heading: S3 Storage Class Selection
concepts.body: S3 Standard suits frequently accessed data at the highest per-GB storage cost, S3 Intelligent-Tiering automatically moves objects between access tiers based on observed access patterns when those patterns are unpredictable, removing the need to manually classify data, and S3 Standard-IA and One Zone-IA suit infrequently accessed data at lower storage cost but with a retrieval fee and, for One Zone-IA, resilience only within a single Availability Zone. The S3 Glacier family (Instant Retrieval, Flexible Retrieval, and Deep Archive) provides progressively cheaper storage in exchange for progressively longer retrieval times, from milliseconds to many hours, and should be matched to how quickly archived data might realistically need to be retrieved.

concepts.heading: AWS Graviton for Price-Performance
concepts.body: AWS Graviton processors are Arm-based and available across EC2, Lambda, RDS, and ElastiCache, typically delivering up to about 40% better price-performance compared to equivalent x86-based instances for compatible workloads. Adopting Graviton usually requires the application (or its container images and dependencies) to support the Arm64 architecture, so the migration effort scales with how much of the software stack needs to be rebuilt or validated for Arm rather than being a simple configuration toggle. For new workloads being designed from scratch, evaluating Graviton compatibility early avoids a costly re-architecture later to capture the same savings.

concepts.heading: Reducing NAT Gateway Costs with VPC Endpoints
concepts.body: NAT Gateway charges are based on both an hourly rate and the volume of data processed through it, which can become a meaningful cost for workloads that make heavy use of AWS services like S3 or DynamoDB from private subnets. Gateway VPC Endpoints for S3 and DynamoDB specifically are free of charge and route that traffic directly over the AWS network instead of through the NAT Gateway, while Interface VPC Endpoints (powered by PrivateLink) cover most other AWS services at an hourly and per-GB cost that is still often lower than the equivalent NAT Gateway processing charge.

examPoints: A requirement to automatically optimize storage cost for data with unpredictable or changing access patterns, without manual lifecycle management, describes S3 Intelligent-Tiering.
A requirement to significantly reduce compute cost for an Arm-compatible workload points to adopting Graviton-based instances.

quiz.q: A new application stores data whose access pattern is unpredictable, sometimes accessed frequently and sometimes not accessed for months, and the team wants storage cost automatically optimized without manual intervention. Which S3 storage class should be used?
choices: Manually moving objects between classes every week
quiz.explain: Intelligent-Tiering automatically moves objects between access tiers based on actual observed usage; S3 Standard alone (choice A) would not reduce cost for infrequently accessed data.

quiz.q: A team is designing a new, Arm-compatible microservice and wants to significantly reduce EC2 compute costs compared to an equivalent x86 instance fleet. What should they use?
quiz.explain: Graviton instances offer up to about 40% better price-performance for compatible workloads; simply switching purchasing options on x86 (choices C and D) does not capture the architecture-level efficiency gain Graviton provides.

days.recap: Cross-AZ and NAT Gateway data transfer both carry real costs that VPC endpoints can reduce, S3 storage classes range from Standard through Intelligent-Tiering and IA to the Glacier tiers based on access frequency and retrieval speed, and Graviton offers meaningful price-performance gains for Arm-compatible new workloads.

days.title: Domain 2 Review — Designing New Solutions

concepts.heading: Building and Deploying New Solutions
concepts.body: Domain 2 begins with how a new solution gets built and shipped: CloudFormation StackSets and CDK for infrastructure as code at scale, and CodePipeline/CodeBuild/CodeDeploy for automated delivery using blue/green (instant rollback, double cost), canary (gradual, monitored rollout), or rolling (resource-efficient, slower rollback) deployment strategies.

concepts.heading: Designing Resilience and Traffic Management from the Start
concepts.body: Because a new solution has no legacy constraints, DR patterns (pilot light, warm standby, multi-site active-active) and traffic management (Route 53's failover/weighted/latency-based/geolocation routing, and Global Accelerator's DNS-independent failover) can be designed in from day one rather than retrofitted.

concepts.heading: Security and Storage Choices for New Applications
concepts.body: New application security combines WAF (layer 7 exploit and bot mitigation), Shield Standard/Advanced (DDoS protection with Advanced adding cost protection and expert support), and Secrets Manager (automated credential rotation). Storage choices span S3 replication (CRR for DR/latency, SRR for aggregation/sovereignty), EFS (elastic shared NFS), and FSx (protocol- and workload-specific managed file systems).

concepts.heading: Compute, Database, and Caching for New Workloads
concepts.body: Compute elasticity relies on Auto Scaling (dynamic, predictive, scheduled) and the right load balancer type (ALB for L7 routing, NLB for L4 performance, GWLB for appliance insertion), often on Fargate to avoid managing EC2 directly. Database choice between Aurora Global Database (single-write-Region, fast promotion) and DynamoDB Global Tables (multi-active writes everywhere) depends on whether every Region needs local writes, and caching layers (CloudFront, ElastiCache, DAX) are matched to what exactly needs to be cached.

concepts.heading: Cost-Conscious Design for New Workloads
concepts.body: New workloads should account for data transfer costs and use VPC endpoints to avoid unnecessary NAT Gateway charges, select S3 storage classes matched to access patterns, and evaluate Graviton compatibility early to capture price-performance gains without a costly later re-architecture.

examPoints: When a Domain 2 scenario says a solution is being built from scratch, treat every constraint (DR, security, database choice) as a design decision to make correctly the first time, not a retrofit.

Watch for scenarios combining a deployment-strategy requirement with a traffic-routing requirement, since blue/green or canary deployments are often paired with Route 53 or Global Accelerator traffic shifting in the same question.

quiz.q: Which deployment strategy allows nearly instant rollback by keeping the previous environment fully running until the new version is validated?
quiz.explain: Blue/green keeps the old environment intact until cutover is confirmed, enabling instant rollback.

quiz.q: Which caching service is purpose-built specifically for DynamoDB and provides microsecond read latency with minimal code changes?
quiz.explain: DAX is DynamoDB-specific and API-compatible with the DynamoDB SDK, unlike the general-purpose ElastiCache.

days.recap: Domain 2 wraps up: designing new solutions means building with IaC and automated CI/CD, designing resilience and traffic routing in from the start, choosing the right security, storage, database, and caching layers, and keeping cost efficiency in mind throughout.

days.title: Operational Excellence: CloudWatch, Systems Manager, and X-Ray

concepts.heading: CloudWatch Metrics, Logs, Alarms, and Anomaly Detection
concepts.body: Amazon CloudWatch unifies metrics, logs, alarms, and dashboards for monitoring existing AWS workloads, and composite alarms let multiple individual alarm conditions be combined with AND/OR logic so a single, more meaningful alert fires only when a genuinely significant combination of conditions occurs, reducing alert fatigue. CloudWatch Anomaly Detection applies machine learning to a metric's historical pattern and creates a dynamic expected range, flagging values that fall outside it even when there is no fixed static threshold that would make sense for a naturally cyclical metric. This is especially useful for metrics with predictable daily or weekly patterns where a single fixed threshold would either miss real anomalies or generate constant false alarms.

concepts.heading: Systems Manager for Fleet-Wide Operations
concepts.body: AWS Systems Manager Run Command executes commands or scripts across large fleets of instances simultaneously without needing SSH access to each one individually, and Patch Manager automates the process of scanning for and applying operating system and application patches on a defined schedule across that same fleet. Systems Manager Automation packages multi-step operational procedures, such as an AMI update workflow or an incident response runbook, into a reusable, auditable automation document rather than relying on tribal knowledge or manual runbooks. Session Manager provides secure, audited shell access to an instance without opening any inbound ports or managing SSH keys, since the session is brokered entirely through the Systems Manager service.

concepts.heading: AWS X-Ray for Distributed Tracing
concepts.body: AWS X-Ray traces a single request as it flows through a distributed, microservices-based application, stitching together the latency and status of each service the request touched into a service map that visually highlights where the bottleneck or error is occurring. This is essential for existing microservices workloads where a slow user-facing response could originate in any one of many backend services, and manually correlating logs across services to find the culprit does not scale. X-Ray requires the application or its SDK to be instrumented to emit trace segments, which is a setup step that distinguishes it from infrastructure-level monitoring like CloudWatch, which requires no application code changes.

concepts.heading: Automating Operational Response
concepts.body: A mature operational practice standardizes repetitive procedures as Systems Manager Automation documents and wires anomaly or threshold detection (CloudWatch Alarms, potentially combined with Anomaly Detection) to EventBridge rules that automatically trigger a Lambda function or Automation runbook, closing the loop between detection and remediation without waiting for a human to notice and act. This reduces mean time to resolution for well-understood, recurring operational issues, freeing engineers to focus on novel problems.

examPoints: A scenario asking to identify which specific microservice is causing latency in a distributed request chain describes AWS X-Ray, not CloudWatch Logs alone.
A scenario asking to automatically apply security patches across hundreds of instances on a schedule describes Systems Manager Patch Manager.

quiz.q: An existing microservices application experiences intermittent slow responses, and the team cannot tell which of a dozen backend services is responsible just from application logs. What should they use?
choices: AWS X-Ray for distributed request tracing
quiz.explain: X-Ray traces individual requests across services and visualizes latency per segment in a service map; CloudWatch Logs alone (choice A) would require manually correlating timestamps across many separate log streams.

quiz.q: An operations team needs to apply security patches automatically to several hundred EC2 instances on a recurring schedule without manually connecting to each one. What should they use?
choices: Recreate each AMI manually every time
quiz.explain: Patch Manager automates scheduled patch scanning and application across large fleets; manual per-instance access (choice A) does not scale to hundreds of instances.

days.recap: CloudWatch unifies metrics/logs/alarms with composite alarms and anomaly detection, Systems Manager provides fleet-wide Run Command/Patch Manager/Automation/Session Manager, and X-Ray traces distributed requests to pinpoint the exact microservice causing latency or errors.

days.title: Automated Security Response: GuardDuty, Security Hub, and EventBridge

concepts.heading: Amazon GuardDuty for Continuous Threat Detection
concepts.body: Amazon GuardDuty continuously analyzes VPC Flow Logs, CloudTrail management and data events, and DNS query logs using machine learning and threat intelligence feeds to detect indicators of compromise, such as an EC2 instance communicating with a known malicious IP address or API calls consistent with credential compromise, without requiring any agent to be installed on monitored resources. Because it operates purely on log and network metadata that AWS already has visibility into, it can be enabled account-wide with a single click, and its findings include a severity score to help prioritize triage. GuardDuty is specifically a detection service; it identifies threats but does not by itself take any remediation action.

concepts.heading: AWS Security Hub CSPM for Centralized Security Posture
concepts.body: AWS Security Hub CSPM (the original AWS Security Hub; the newer unified AWS Security Hub builds on it to correlate and prioritize findings) aggregates findings from GuardDuty, Inspector, Macie, and other supported security services (plus third-party integrations) into one centralized dashboard, and also runs automated checks against security standards like the CIS AWS Foundations Benchmark or PCI DSS to continuously score compliance posture. This is the tool for a scenario needing a single pane of glass across multiple security services' findings rather than checking each service's console separately, and it can aggregate findings across an entire AWS Organization when deployed with a delegated administrator account.

concepts.heading: Automated Remediation with EventBridge and Lambda
concepts.body: A standard automated-remediation pattern routes a GuardDuty or Security Hub finding as an event through Amazon EventBridge, which matches it against a rule and invokes a Lambda function that takes an immediate remediation action, such as isolating a compromised instance by swapping its security group to a locked-down one, revoking temporary credentials, or disabling an IAM key, all without waiting for a human responder. This closes the gap between detection and containment from potentially hours down to seconds, which matters most for fast-moving threats like credential exfiltration or crypto-mining malware that spreads or causes damage quickly.

concepts.heading: Compliance Remediation Beyond Threat Detection
concepts.body: The same EventBridge-triggered Lambda remediation pattern applies to compliance drift, not just active threats: an AWS Config rule detecting a non-compliant resource (such as an unencrypted EBS volume or a publicly readable S3 bucket) can trigger Config Remediation or a custom Lambda function to automatically bring the resource back into compliance, and Secrets Manager's own scheduled rotation is itself a specialized case of this same automate-the-response philosophy applied to credential hygiene.

examPoints: A scenario describing detection of threats from VPC Flow Logs, CloudTrail, and DNS logs via machine learning, with no agent installation, describes GuardDuty.
A scenario describing automatic, human-free isolation of a compromised instance immediately after a threat is detected describes an EventBridge rule triggering a Lambda remediation function.

quiz.q: A security team wants to continuously detect threats such as command-and-control traffic and credential misuse across their AWS accounts by analyzing VPC Flow Logs, CloudTrail, and DNS logs, without installing any agents. Which service should they enable?
quiz.explain: GuardDuty analyzes these log sources with machine learning and requires no agents; AWS Config (choice A) tracks resource configuration state, not network threat activity.

quiz.q: A company wants a compromised EC2 instance to be automatically isolated the moment GuardDuty detects malicious activity on it, without waiting for a security analyst to respond manually. What architecture achieves this?
choices: Email the security team and wait for manual action
GuardDuty finding triggers an EventBridge rule that invokes a Lambda function to isolate the instance
Rely on Security Hub's dashboard alone
Disable the instance's IAM role only
quiz.explain: Routing the finding through EventBridge to a Lambda function enables immediate, automated remediation; a dashboard alone (choice C) still requires a human to notice and act.

days.recap: GuardDuty continuously detects threats with machine learning and no agents, Security Hub CSPM aggregates findings and scores compliance across multiple security services in one dashboard, and EventBridge plus Lambda automates rapid, human-free remediation for both security threats and compliance drift.

days.title: Performance Tuning for Existing Workloads: Global Accelerator, CloudFront, and Auto Scaling

concepts.heading: Improving Global Latency for Existing Applications
concepts.body: For an existing application experiencing latency complaints from geographically distant users, Global Accelerator can be layered in to route traffic over the AWS backbone via the nearest edge location without requiring any application redesign, and CloudFront's cache hit ratio can be improved by tuning TTL settings and cache key configuration so that more requests are served directly from the edge rather than round-tripping to the origin. Both of these are largely non-invasive performance improvements that can be applied to an already-running application with minimal architectural change, which is a defining trait of Domain 3 scenarios versus Domain 2's from-scratch design.

concepts.heading: Tuning Auto Scaling for Faster, Smarter Response
concepts.body: An existing Auto Scaling group's cooldown period, the time it waits after a scaling activity before considering another one, can be tuned to better match the workload's actual burst pattern, avoiding both premature re-scaling and sluggish response to sustained load changes. Target tracking scaling policies let an operator refine which metric (CPU, request count per target, or a custom metric) and what target value drives scaling decisions, making reactive scaling more precise over time as real traffic patterns become better understood. A warm pool keeps a set of pre-initialized instances in a stopped or running state ready to be added to the group quickly, cutting the time needed to actually add capacity during a scale-out event, which matters most for instances with slow boot or application warm-up times.

concepts.heading: RDS Performance Improvements
concepts.body: For an existing RDS or Aurora database showing signs of strain, adding read replicas offloads read-heavy query traffic from the primary instance, directly increasing available read capacity without vertically scaling the primary. RDS Performance Insights visualizes database load over time and breaks it down by SQL statement, wait event, user, or host, making it possible to pinpoint a specific slow or resource-heavy query that is the actual bottleneck rather than guessing from aggregate CPU or IOPS metrics alone. Parameter group tuning, adjusting engine-specific settings like buffer pool size or connection limits, is a further lever once the specific bottleneck has been identified.

concepts.heading: Continuous Compute and Cost-Performance Review
concepts.body: Performance improvement for existing workloads is an ongoing practice, not a one-time project: periodically re-evaluating instance types (including migrating to Graviton where compatible) and re-running Compute Optimizer recommendations as usage patterns evolve ensures that performance and cost efficiency keep pace with how the application's actual traffic and resource needs change over time.

examPoints: A scenario describing a need to reduce instance boot-time delay during Auto Scaling scale-out events describes a warm pool.
A scenario asking to identify which specific SQL query is the bottleneck in an existing RDS database describes RDS Performance Insights.

quiz.q: An existing application's Auto Scaling group takes several minutes to add capacity during traffic spikes because new instances have a slow boot and application initialization process. What should reduce this scale-out latency?
choices: Use a warm pool of pre-initialized instances
quiz.explain: A warm pool keeps instances pre-initialized and ready to join the group quickly; increasing the cooldown period (choice A) would only slow down further scaling actions, not speed up the initial one.

quiz.q: An existing RDS database shows high CPU utilization, but the team does not know which specific query is responsible. What should they use to identify the exact bottleneck query?
quiz.explain: Performance Insights breaks down database load by SQL statement and wait event, directly identifying the bottleneck; CloudTrail (choice A) records API calls, not database query performance.

days.recap: Global latency for existing workloads improves with Global Accelerator and CloudFront cache tuning, Auto Scaling tuning uses cooldowns, target tracking, and warm pools, RDS gains from read replicas and Performance Insights query-level diagnosis, and ongoing instance-type and Graviton review keeps performance and cost aligned over time.

days.title: Improving Reliability: Eliminating Single Points of Failure and Chaos Engineering with FIS

concepts.heading: Identifying and Eliminating Single Points of Failure
concepts.body: A single point of failure (SPOF) is any component whose failure alone can take down the whole system, and common examples in an existing architecture include a single-AZ deployment, one NAT Gateway serving an entire private subnet's outbound traffic, or a database running as a single, non-redundant instance. Eliminating an SPOF generally means adding redundancy in the same dimension the failure could occur, for example deploying one NAT Gateway per Availability Zone rather than a single shared one, so a single AZ's NAT Gateway failure only affects that one AZ's outbound traffic rather than the entire application.

concepts.heading: AWS Fault Injection Simulator for Controlled Chaos Engineering
concepts.body: AWS Fault Injection Simulator (FIS) runs controlled experiments that intentionally inject real failure conditions, such as terminating an instance, throttling an API, injecting network latency, or simulating an entire Availability Zone outage, into a system to validate that its resilience mechanisms actually work as designed before a real, uncontrolled failure occurs. This proactive validation is valuable because resilience mechanisms like Auto Scaling health checks or Multi-AZ failover are often configured but never actually tested end-to-end until an unplanned real incident forces the issue, by which point it's too late to fix a gap safely. FIS experiments are scoped and time-boxed with stop conditions, so an experiment can be automatically halted if it causes more impact than intended.

concepts.heading: Circuit Breakers and Exponential Backoff with Jitter
concepts.body: A circuit breaker pattern stops an application from repeatedly calling a downstream service that is already failing, quickly failing the calling request instead of waiting on a timeout every time, which prevents a struggling downstream service from being made worse by continued load and prevents the failure from cascading upstream. Retrying with exponential backoff and jitter (randomizing the wait time between retries) prevents many clients from retrying in synchronized bursts that would otherwise create a thundering-herd effect against a recovering service, spreading retry load out more evenly over time.

concepts.heading: Health Checks and Automatic Replacement
concepts.body: Elastic Load Balancing health checks continuously probe registered targets and automatically stop routing traffic to any target that fails, preventing users from being sent to a broken instance, while an Auto Scaling group's own health checks go a step further by automatically terminating and replacing an unhealthy instance entirely. Together, these two mechanisms form the baseline self-healing behavior that most resilient architectures depend on, and FIS experiments are frequently designed specifically to validate that this self-healing chain actually functions as expected under real failure conditions.

examPoints: A scenario asking to intentionally and safely inject a real failure, such as an Availability Zone outage, to validate resilience before it happens for real describes AWS Fault Injection Simulator.

A scenario describing an outage of an entire Availability Zone taking down all outbound internet access for private subnets because only one NAT Gateway exists describes a single point of failure that should be resolved by deploying one NAT Gateway per AZ.

quiz.q: A team wants to validate, before a real incident happens, that their application actually survives the simulated loss of an entire Availability Zone. What should they use?
choices: Manually shut down servers in production with no plan
AWS Fault Injection Simulator to run a controlled, scoped experiment
Just monitor CloudWatch and hope for the best
Skip validation since Multi-AZ is already configured
quiz.explain: FIS is designed for exactly this kind of controlled chaos engineering experiment with defined stop conditions; skipping validation (choice D) leaves an untested assumption about the resilience configuration.

quiz.q: An application's private subnets in a particular Availability Zone lose all outbound internet access whenever that AZ's single NAT Gateway has an issue, since it is the only NAT Gateway in the VPC. What is the correct fix?
choices: Leave the NAT Gateway as is
Deploy one NAT Gateway per Availability Zone
quiz.explain: Deploying a NAT Gateway per AZ eliminates this single point of failure by scoping the impact of any one NAT Gateway's failure to just its own AZ.

days.recap: Eliminate SPOFs by adding redundancy such as per-AZ NAT Gateways, use FIS to proactively and safely validate resilience mechanisms before a real failure occurs, apply circuit breakers and exponential backoff with jitter to prevent cascading failures, and rely on ELB and Auto Scaling health checks for automatic detection and replacement.

days.title: Optimizing Costs on Existing Systems: Trusted Advisor and Rightsizing

concepts.heading: AWS Trusted Advisor's Five Check Categories
concepts.body: AWS Trusted Advisor automatically checks an account against AWS best practices across five categories: cost optimization (identifying idle or underutilized resources like low-utilization EC2 instances and unattached Elastic IP addresses), performance, security, fault tolerance, and service limits (quota usage approaching a hard ceiling). This gives a broad, automated first pass across an existing environment without requiring a manual audit of every resource, and full check coverage requires a Business or Enterprise support plan, with a smaller free set of checks available to all customers.

concepts.heading: Rightsizing with Compute Optimizer Recommendations
concepts.body: Rightsizing an existing fleet means using Compute Optimizer's data-driven recommendations, based on actual historical CPU, memory, and network utilization, to move over-provisioned instances to a smaller size or to a more cost-effective instance family, such as moving from a general-purpose family to a compute-optimized one when the workload is consistently CPU-bound. This is a recurring exercise for existing systems, since workload characteristics and AWS's available instance types both change over time, meaning a rightsizing decision made a year ago may no longer be optimal today.

concepts.heading: Identifying Savings Plans and RI Coverage Gaps
concepts.body: Cost Explorer's Savings Plans and Reserved Instance coverage and utilization reports show what percentage of existing steady-state On-Demand usage is not yet covered by a commitment-based discount, surfacing additional savings opportunities in workloads that have proven stable enough over time to justify a one- or three-year commitment retroactively. This is specifically about identifying existing On-Demand spend that should be converted, distinct from Compute Optimizer's rightsizing recommendations, which are about right-sizing the instance itself regardless of purchasing option.

concepts.heading: S3 Storage Lens for Organization-Wide Storage Insight
concepts.body: S3 Storage Lens analyzes storage usage and activity trends across an entire organization's S3 buckets and accounts, surfacing cost optimization opportunities such as buckets accumulating old, rarely accessed objects that are still sitting in an expensive storage class, or buckets that would benefit from a lifecycle policy. This organization-wide view is valuable for existing systems specifically because storage usage patterns tend to drift silently over months or years without anyone actively monitoring them, unlike compute costs which are typically more visible.

examPoints: A scenario asking to broadly identify idle or underutilized resources (low-utilization instances, unattached Elastic IPs) across an entire account points to Trusted Advisor's cost optimization checks.
A scenario asking to analyze S3 usage patterns across an entire organization to find inefficient storage classes or old unused objects points to S3 Storage Lens.

quiz.q: A company wants a broad, automated first pass across its account to identify idle EC2 instances, unattached Elastic IPs, and other cost-saving opportunities without manually reviewing every resource. What should it use?
choices: AWS Trusted Advisor's cost optimization checks
Ignoring cost until the bill arrives
quiz.explain: Trusted Advisor automatically checks for idle and underutilized resources across the account; manual review (choice A) does not scale and is slower to surface these findings.

quiz.q: A company wants to analyze S3 usage patterns across its entire organization to find inefficient storage classes and old, rarely accessed objects. What should it use?
quiz.explain: Storage Lens is purpose-built for organization-wide S3 usage pattern analysis and cost optimization opportunities.

days.recap: Trusted Advisor checks five best-practice categories including cost optimization for idle resources, rightsizing uses Compute Optimizer's data-driven recommendations, Savings Plans coverage analysis finds additional commitment-based savings opportunities, and S3 Storage Lens surfaces organization-wide storage cost inefficiencies.

days.title: Refactoring Toward Loose Coupling: SQS, SNS, and EventBridge

concepts.heading: The Problem with Tight Coupling
concepts.body: In a tightly coupled architecture, a failure or slowdown in one component propagates directly and immediately to whatever calls it synchronously, meaning a single struggling downstream service can cause a cascading failure across the entire system. Tightly coupled architectures also scale poorly, since every component must be sized to handle the immediate, synchronous demands of every other component calling it, rather than being able to process work at its own independent pace.

concepts.heading: Amazon SQS for Asynchronous Decoupling
concepts.body: Amazon SQS decouples a producer from a consumer by placing messages in a durable queue between them, so the producer can continue working even if the consumer is temporarily slow, unavailable, or overwhelmed, since messages simply wait in the queue until the consumer catches up. Standard queues offer nearly unlimited throughput with at-least-once delivery and best-effort ordering, while FIFO queues guarantee strict ordering and exactly-once processing within a message group at somewhat lower throughput, so the choice depends on whether the workload can tolerate occasional duplicates and out-of-order processing.

concepts.heading: Amazon SNS for Pub/Sub Fan-Out
concepts.body: Amazon SNS implements a publish-subscribe model where a single published message can be delivered to many different subscriber types simultaneously, including SQS queues, Lambda functions, HTTP endpoints, email, and SMS, without the publisher needing any knowledge of who the subscribers are. The SNS-to-multiple-SQS fan-out pattern is especially common: SNS publishes once, and each subscribing SQS queue receives its own independent copy of the message, letting multiple downstream consumers process the same event independently and durably, each at their own pace, without any consumer's slowness affecting the others.

concepts.heading: Amazon EventBridge for Event-Driven Integration
concepts.body: Amazon EventBridge is a serverless event bus that can ingest events from AWS services, SaaS partners, and custom applications, and route them to targets based on fine-grained event pattern rules that match on the event's actual content, not just its source. This makes EventBridge particularly well suited to refactoring a monolith into event-driven, loosely coupled services, since new consumers can subscribe to relevant events without the event producer needing to change at all, unlike a tightly coupled direct-call integration where adding a new consumer requires modifying the producer's code.

examPoints: A scenario describing a need to prevent a temporarily failing downstream microservice from cascading failure to an upstream service describes asynchronous decoupling with SQS.
A scenario describing one event needing to reliably reach multiple independent subscribers (such as SQS, Lambda, and email) at once describes the SNS pub/sub fan-out pattern.

quiz.q: An existing monolithic order-processing service occasionally experiences slowdowns that cascade and cause failures in the payment service that calls it synchronously. How should this be refactored to prevent cascading failure?
choices: Add more synchronous retries to the payment service
Introduce an SQS queue between the two services for asynchronous processing
Merge both services into one to avoid the call entirely
Reduce the timeout on the synchronous call
quiz.explain: An SQS queue decouples the two services asynchronously so a slowdown in one does not directly cascade to the other; more synchronous retries (choice A) would worsen the cascading effect under load.

quiz.q: A single order-placed event needs to reliably reach an email confirmation Lambda function, an inventory-update SQS queue, and an analytics pipeline, all independently. What pattern fits best?
choices: Direct synchronous calls from the order service to each consumer
SNS publishing to multiple independent SQS subscribers (fan-out)
A single SQS queue shared by all three consumers
Polling a database table from each consumer
quiz.explain: SNS fan-out delivers an independent copy of the message to each subscriber, letting each process at its own pace; a single shared queue (choice C) would have consumers competing for the same messages instead of each receiving its own copy.

days.recap: Tight coupling risks cascading failure, SQS asynchronously decouples producers from consumers (standard for throughput, FIFO for ordering), SNS fans one message out to many independent subscribers, and EventBridge routes content-filtered events between AWS services, SaaS, and custom apps for loosely coupled integration.

days.title: Observability and Troubleshooting: CloudTrail, VPC Flow Logs, and Config

concepts.heading: AWS CloudTrail for API Auditing
concepts.body: AWS CloudTrail records every API call made within an account, distinguishing management events (control-plane operations like creating or modifying resources, enabled by default) from data events (higher-volume operations like S3 object-level GetObject/PutObject calls or DynamoDB item-level access, which must be explicitly enabled and incur additional cost because of their volume). An organization trail extends this logging across every account in an AWS Organization automatically, centralizing audit logs from all member accounts into one designated logging location rather than requiring each account to configure its own trail independently.

concepts.heading: VPC Flow Logs for Network-Level Diagnosis
concepts.body: VPC Flow Logs capture metadata about IP traffic flowing through network interfaces in a VPC, subnet, or individual elastic network interface, recording whether traffic was accepted or rejected along with source, destination, port, and protocol, without capturing the actual packet payload. This is the primary tool for diagnosing whether a connectivity failure is caused by a security group or network ACL blocking traffic versus some other application-layer issue, since Flow Logs show definitively whether the traffic was even allowed to reach its destination at the network layer.

concepts.heading: AWS Config for Configuration History and Continuous Compliance
concepts.body: AWS Config maintains a timeline of exactly how a resource's configuration has changed over time, which supports both point-in-time troubleshooting (what did this security group look like last Tuesday) and audit requirements, and Config Rules continuously evaluate resources against a desired configuration, flagging or, with Config Remediation, automatically correcting drift from that policy. Config's focus on resulting configuration state is what distinguishes it from CloudTrail's focus on the API calls that caused changes; the two together answer both who made a change and what the resulting state actually was.

concepts.heading: Matching the Right Log Source to the Problem
concepts.body: Effective troubleshooting starts by matching the type of problem to the right log source: application-level errors and latency point to CloudWatch Logs and X-Ray, network connectivity failures point to VPC Flow Logs plus a review of security groups and NACLs, questions about who changed what and when point to CloudTrail, and questions about how a resource's configuration evolved over time or whether it's currently compliant point to Config. Recognizing which category a scenario's troubleshooting question falls into is usually the fastest path to the correct answer.

examPoints: A scenario asking to log individual S3 object-level access (GetObject/PutObject) for detailed audit purposes describes CloudTrail data events, which must be explicitly enabled.

A scenario asking whether a failed connection to an instance was blocked by a security group or NACL, versus some other issue, describes using VPC Flow Logs to check whether the traffic was accepted or rejected.

quiz.q: A compliance team needs to log every individual object-level access (GetObject and PutObject calls) on a specific S3 bucket for audit purposes. What must they configure?
choices: CloudTrail management events, which are enabled by default
CloudTrail data events, explicitly enabled for that bucket
quiz.explain: Object-level S3 access is recorded through CloudTrail data events, which are not enabled by default and must be turned on explicitly; management events (choice A) only cover control-plane operations.

quiz.q: An application team reports that connections to a specific EC2 instance are failing, and they are unsure if it's due to a security group misconfiguration or a different network issue. What should they check first?
choices: VPC Flow Logs to see if the traffic was accepted or rejected
quiz.explain: VPC Flow Logs directly show whether traffic reached the instance and whether it was accepted or rejected at the network layer, quickly narrowing down the cause.

days.recap: CloudTrail audits API calls (management events by default, data events must be enabled), VPC Flow Logs record network traffic accept/reject decisions for connectivity diagnosis, Config tracks configuration history and continuous compliance, and matching the problem type to the right log source speeds up troubleshooting.

days.title: Domain 3 Review — Continuous Improvement

concepts.heading: Operational Tooling for Existing Workloads
concepts.body: Domain 3 opens with the operational toolkit for systems already running in production: CloudWatch (metrics, logs, alarms, anomaly detection), Systems Manager (Run Command, Patch Manager, Automation, Session Manager), and X-Ray (distributed tracing to pinpoint microservice bottlenecks), all aimed at understanding and maintaining an existing system rather than designing a new one.

concepts.heading: Automated Security Response for Running Systems
concepts.body: Security improvement for existing workloads pairs GuardDuty's agentless, machine-learning-based threat detection and Security Hub CSPM's centralized findings aggregation and compliance scoring with EventBridge-triggered Lambda remediation, closing the gap between detecting a threat or compliance violation and actually containing or fixing it, often within seconds rather than hours.

concepts.heading: Performance and Reliability Improvement
concepts.body: Performance tuning for existing workloads layers Global Accelerator and CloudFront cache optimization, Auto Scaling tuning (cooldowns, target tracking, warm pools), and RDS read replicas plus Performance Insights on top of an already-running architecture with minimal redesign. Reliability improvement means finding and eliminating single points of failure and using AWS Fault Injection Simulator to proactively validate that resilience mechanisms actually work before a real failure forces the issue.

concepts.heading: Cost Optimization and Architectural Refactoring
concepts.body: Cost optimization for existing systems combines Trusted Advisor's automated best-practice checks, Compute Optimizer-driven rightsizing, Savings Plans coverage analysis, and S3 Storage Lens for organization-wide storage insight. Architectural refactoring moves tightly coupled, cascading-failure-prone designs toward loose coupling using SQS for asynchronous decoupling, SNS for pub/sub fan-out, and EventBridge for content-filtered event-driven integration.

concepts.heading: Diagnosing Problems in a Running System
concepts.body: Observability rounds out Domain 3: CloudTrail for API-level audit, VPC Flow Logs for network-level connectivity diagnosis, and Config for configuration history and continuous compliance evaluation, each matched to a distinct category of troubleshooting question.

examPoints: When a Domain 3 scenario says 'existing' or 'currently running,' expect the correct answer to be an improvement layered onto the current architecture rather than a from-scratch redesign, which is the key signal distinguishing Domain 3 from Domain 2.
Separate diagnosis from remediation in Domain 3 scenarios: first identify which log or tool reveals the root cause, then separately identify which service applies the fix.

quiz.q: Which AWS service traces a single request across multiple microservices to identify which one is causing latency in an existing distributed application?
quiz.explain: X-Ray traces distributed requests across services and visualizes latency bottlenecks in a service map.

quiz.q: What is the standard architecture for automatically responding to a detected security threat without human intervention?
choices: GuardDuty finding routed through EventBridge to a Lambda remediation function
Strengthening IAM policies only, with no automation
quiz.explain: Routing the detection through EventBridge to Lambda is the standard automated-remediation pattern for a rapid, human-free response.

days.recap: Domain 3 wraps up: continuously improving an existing workload means diagnosing (logs and tools) and improving (applying the right service) operations, security, performance, reliability, cost, and architecture in an ongoing cycle rather than a one-time project.

days.title: Migration Readiness: Discovery with AWS Transform, Migration Evaluator, and the 7 Rs

concepts.heading: Discovery and Dependency Mapping with AWS Transform
concepts.body: AWS Transform, the recommended alternative to AWS Application Discovery Service (closed to new customers since 2025-11-07), automatically discovers on-premises servers (VMware, Hyper-V, or bare metal) through a discovery appliance deployed in the data center and collects server specifications, utilization data, and network dependencies, then uses them to group applications and plan migration waves. This dependency data is the foundation of any large-scale migration plan, since migrating a server without knowing what else depends on it, or what it depends on, risks breaking connected systems that were never accounted for; migrating a group of tightly interdependent servers separately, out of order, is a common and costly planning mistake this data prevents.

concepts.heading: AWS Migration Evaluator for Business Case Development
concepts.body: AWS Migration Evaluator uses collected on-premises utilization data to build a data-driven cost projection for what an equivalent workload would cost to run on AWS, which supports building an ROI-based business case for migration funding before any actual migration work begins. This is distinct from the dependency-mapping purpose of discovery in AWS Transform; Migration Evaluator answers 'what will this cost and save us,' while discovery answers 'what do we have and how is it connected.'

concepts.heading: The 7 Rs Migration Strategies
concepts.body: The 7 Rs framework categorizes how to treat each application during migration: Retire (decommission an application no longer needed), Retain (keep it on-premises for now, often due to compliance or a recent investment), Rehost (lift-and-shift with minimal to no code changes), Relocate (move at the hypervisor level, commonly used for VMware workloads moving to VMware Cloud on AWS), Repurchase (replace with a SaaS alternative), Replatform (make targeted optimizations, such as moving to a managed database, while migrating with limited code changes), and Reengineer/Refactor (rearchitect the application to take full advantage of cloud-native capabilities). Choosing the right R for a given application balances migration speed and cost against how much cloud-native benefit is captured.

concepts.heading: Centralized Migration Planning and Tracking
concepts.body: AWS Migration Hub (closed to new customers since 2025-11-07; AWS recommends AWS Transform, which now offers its features) provided a single dashboard to track the status and progress of migrations being executed across multiple underlying AWS migration tools, including DMS for databases, MGN for servers, and SCT for schema conversion, so a program manager overseeing a large migration involving many applications and tools did not have to check each tool's own console separately to understand overall progress.

examPoints: A scenario describing the need to understand dependencies between hundreds of on-premises servers before planning a safe migration sequence describes automated discovery and dependency mapping, done today with AWS Transform (older questions may name Application Discovery Service, closed to new customers since 2025-11-07).
A scenario describing moving an application to the cloud as quickly as possible with no code changes describes the Rehost (lift-and-shift) strategy among the 7 Rs.

quiz.q: A company is planning to migrate hundreds of on-premises servers and needs to understand their dependencies and utilization before deciding on a safe migration order. What should it use first?
choices: AWS Transform to discover the servers and map their configuration and dependencies
quiz.explain: AWS Transform discovery (the recommended alternative to Application Discovery Service, closed to new customers since 2025-11-07) collects the dependency and utilization data needed to plan a safe migration sequence; starting without this analysis (choice A) risks breaking interdependent systems.

quiz.q: An application needs to move to the cloud with minimal changes and as quickly as possible, with optimization deferred until after migration. Which of the 7 Rs strategies fits this?
quiz.explain: Rehost moves an application with minimal to no changes, prioritizing migration speed over immediate optimization.

days.recap: AWS Transform discovers on-premises configuration and dependency data (replacing Application Discovery Service and Migration Hub, both closed to new customers since 2025-11-07), Migration Evaluator builds a data-driven cost projection for the business case, and the 7 Rs (Retire, Retain, Rehost, Relocate, Repurchase, Replatform, Reengineer) categorize migration approach per application.

days.title: Migrating Data at Scale: DataSync, Offline Transfer, and Transfer Family

concepts.heading: AWS DataSync for Online Data Transfer
concepts.body: AWS DataSync moves large amounts of data online between on-premises NFS or SMB file servers and AWS storage services like S3, EFS, or FSx, using parallel, multi-threaded transfer and automatic data integrity verification to move data quickly and reliably over an existing network connection. DataSync also supports ongoing, scheduled synchronization rather than just a one-time transfer, making it suitable for keeping an AWS copy of on-premises data continuously up to date during a phased migration rather than only for a single cutover event.

concepts.heading: Offline Data Transfer: From the Snow Family to AWS Data Transfer Terminal
concepts.body: When the volume of data to migrate is large enough, or available network bandwidth low enough, that an online transfer would take weeks or months, data has to move physically instead. The AWS Snow Family did this by shipping a rugged device to the customer, but it is no longer an option for new customers: Snowcone was discontinued in 2024-11, Snowmobile was retired in 2024, and Snowball Edge has been closed to new customers since 2025-11-07 (older exam questions may still name it). AWS now recommends AWS Data Transfer Terminal, a reserved AWS facility where the customer brings its own storage devices and uploads over a high-bandwidth connection straight to S3 or EFS, or an AWS Partner solution; AWS Outposts covers the edge-compute use cases Snowball Edge used to serve.

concepts.heading: Deciding Between Online and Offline Transfer
concepts.body: The standard rule of thumb for choosing between DataSync and an offline transfer is to estimate how long an online transfer would take given the available network bandwidth and the data volume; if that estimate stretches into many weeks, loading the data onto physical storage and uploading it at an AWS Data Transfer Terminal, faster than the equivalent online transfer, becomes the more practical and often more cost-effective choice. This calculation, rather than data volume alone, is what the exam expects a candidate to reason through when choosing between the two approaches.

concepts.heading: AWS Transfer Family for Legacy Protocol Compatibility
concepts.body: AWS Transfer Family provides fully managed support for SFTP, FTPS, and FTP protocols, letting existing partner or internal workflows that depend on these legacy file-transfer protocols continue operating unchanged while the underlying storage moves to S3 or EFS. This matters for migrations where changing the file transfer protocol itself is not feasible in the short term, such as an established B2B data exchange process with an external partner that specifically requires SFTP and cannot be easily changed to a modern API-based integration.

examPoints: A scenario describing hundreds of terabytes of data that would take months to transfer over the available network bandwidth describes needing an offline, physical transfer (AWS Data Transfer Terminal for new customers; older questions may name a Snow Family device) rather than an online transfer tool.
A scenario describing an on-premises NFS file server that needs its data continuously and incrementally synchronized to S3 during a phased migration describes AWS DataSync.

quiz.q: A company estimates that transferring 500 TB of data over its available network connection would take several months, delaying a migration deadline. What is the most efficient way to move this data to AWS?
choices: Continue the online transfer regardless of time
Load the data onto storage devices and upload it at an AWS Data Transfer Terminal
Reduce the amount of data being migrated
Use a smaller file server and a proxy
quiz.explain: When bandwidth-constrained online transfer would take an impractically long time, moving the data physically is the more efficient approach; for new customers that means AWS Data Transfer Terminal (or a Partner solution), since Snowball Edge has been closed to new customers since 2025-11-07.

quiz.q: A company needs to continuously and incrementally synchronize data from an on-premises NFS file server to Amazon S3 throughout a multi-month, phased migration. What should it use?
quiz.explain: DataSync supports online, ongoing scheduled synchronization between NFS/SMB sources and S3/EFS/FSx; Snowmobile (choice A, retired in 2024) was a one-time offline bulk transfer solution, not for ongoing sync.

days.recap: DataSync moves and continuously syncs large datasets online between on-premises file servers and AWS storage, AWS Data Transfer Terminal moves data offline when bandwidth makes online transfer impractical (the Snow Family is no longer available to new customers), the choice depends on estimated transfer time versus data volume, and Transfer Family preserves legacy SFTP/FTPS/FTP workflows against S3 or EFS.

days.title: Rehosting Servers at Scale with AWS Application Migration Service

concepts.heading: How AWS Application Migration Service (MGN) Works
concepts.body: AWS Application Migration Service (MGN) is AWS's recommended rehosting tool, working by installing a lightweight replication agent on each source server (on-premises or on another cloud) that continuously replicates disk blocks to a staging area in AWS, keeping the AWS copy nearly current with the live source server at all times. Because replication is continuous rather than a one-time snapshot, the actual cutover to AWS involves only a brief final synchronization, minimizing downtime compared to a traditional migration approach that copies data once and then requires an extended maintenance window.

concepts.heading: The Replicate, Test, Cutover Workflow
concepts.body: MGN's migration workflow follows three stages: continuous replication keeps the staging-area copy current with minimal ongoing overhead on the source server, launching a test instance from the replicated data lets the team validate the migrated server actually boots and functions correctly in AWS without affecting the still-running production source, and cutover performs the final switch, redirecting production traffic to the now-migrated AWS instance once testing has confirmed it works. Running the test step repeatedly, without disrupting the source server, is one of MGN's key advantages over migration approaches that require taking the source offline to validate a copy.

concepts.heading: MGN vs. Elastic Disaster Recovery (DRS)
concepts.body: MGN and Elastic Disaster Recovery share the same underlying continuous block-level replication technology, but they serve different purposes: MGN is used for a one-time migration, and replication is stopped once the cutover to AWS is complete, while DRS is used for ongoing disaster recovery, where replication continues indefinitely so a recovery instance can be launched at any future point if the source ever fails. Recognizing this shared-technology-but-different-purpose relationship is a frequently tested exam distinction.

concepts.heading: Migration Wave Planning
concepts.body: Large-scale server migrations are typically organized into waves, grouping applications by their dependencies (using discovery data from AWS Transform, the recommended alternative to Application Discovery Service, which has been closed to new customers since 2025-11-07) so that tightly interdependent servers are migrated together within the same wave, while independent, low-risk applications are migrated in earlier waves to build confidence and refine the process before tackling more complex, interdependent systems later.

examPoints: A scenario describing the need to migrate hundreds of on-premises servers to AWS with minimal downtime, using continuous replication and a validated cutover, describes AWS Application Migration Service (MGN).
A scenario distinguishing a one-time migration project from an ongoing disaster recovery capability, despite using the same replication technology, is testing the MGN-versus-DRS distinction.

quiz.q: A company needs to migrate several hundred on-premises servers to AWS with minimal downtime, using AWS's recommended tool for large-scale, automated server rehosting. What should it use?
choices: Manually rebuild each server from scratch in AWS
quiz.explain: MGN is purpose-built for large-scale, minimal-downtime server rehosting through continuous replication; manual rebuilding (choice A) does not scale to hundreds of servers.

quiz.q: What is the key difference between AWS Application Migration Service (MGN) and AWS Elastic Disaster Recovery (DRS), given that both use the same underlying replication technology?
choices: There is no difference between them
MGN is for a one-time migration; DRS is for ongoing disaster recovery
MGN is for databases only; DRS is for servers only
DRS is for migration only; MGN is for disaster recovery only
quiz.explain: The two services share replication technology but differ in purpose: MGN stops replication after a one-time cutover, while DRS maintains replication indefinitely for ongoing DR readiness.

days.recap: MGN performs continuous block-level replication for minimal-downtime rehosting, its workflow is replicate, test, then cutover, MGN (one-time migration) and DRS (ongoing DR) share the same underlying technology for different purposes, and migration waves group applications by dependency to sequence a large-scale migration safely.

days.title: Database Migration: DMS and the Schema Conversion Tool

concepts.heading: AWS Database Migration Service Fundamentals
concepts.body: AWS Database Migration Service (DMS) migrates data from a source database to a target database, supporting both a one-time full load of existing data and ongoing change data capture (CDC) that continuously replicates new changes made to the source after the full load completes, keeping the target current with the live source. DMS supports both homogeneous migrations (same database engine on both sides) and heterogeneous migrations (different engines), though the schema itself is not converted by DMS in the heterogeneous case; only the data is moved once a compatible target schema already exists.

concepts.heading: Homogeneous vs. Heterogeneous Migrations
concepts.body: A homogeneous migration, such as Oracle to Oracle or MySQL to Aurora MySQL, moves data between database engines with essentially the same schema structure, stored procedure language, and data types, so DMS alone is typically sufficient without any schema transformation step. A heterogeneous migration, such as Oracle to Aurora PostgreSQL, involves fundamentally different schema structures, data types, and procedural code (like stored procedures and functions written in a different SQL dialect), which DMS itself does not translate, making a separate schema and code conversion step a required first step before DMS can move any data.

concepts.heading: AWS Schema Conversion Tool (SCT) for Heterogeneous Migrations
concepts.body: The AWS Schema Conversion Tool (SCT) analyzes a source database's schema and automatically converts it, along with stored procedures, functions, and views, to an equivalent schema compatible with the target database engine, flagging any objects that cannot be automatically converted and require manual rework. The standard heterogeneous migration workflow runs SCT first to produce a compatible target schema, then runs DMS to move the actual data (with CDC for minimal downtime), rather than running the two tools in the opposite order or expecting either tool alone to complete the migration.

concepts.heading: Using CDC for a Minimal-Downtime Cutover
concepts.body: The full-load-then-CDC pattern lets a production database keep running and accepting writes throughout most of the migration: DMS performs an initial full load of existing data while the source remains fully operational, then CDC continuously captures and applies ongoing changes made to the source during that time, and only a brief final synchronization window (rather than the full data volume) is needed at actual cutover, minimizing the production downtime required to complete the migration.

examPoints: A scenario describing migration between two different database engines with different schema structures and stored procedure languages describes needing SCT for schema conversion before DMS moves the data.
A scenario describing a production database that must remain available and current throughout most of a migration, with only a brief final cutover window, describes DMS's full-load-plus-CDC pattern.

quiz.q: A company is migrating from Oracle to Aurora PostgreSQL, and the two databases have significantly different schema structures and stored procedure languages. What is the correct migration approach?
choices: Use DMS alone to migrate both schema and data
Use SCT to convert the schema and stored procedures first, then use DMS to migrate the data
Manually rewrite everything with no tooling
Use DataSync to copy the database files directly
quiz.explain: SCT handles heterogeneous schema and code conversion, which DMS itself does not perform; DMS alone (choice A) cannot translate between fundamentally different schema structures and dialects.

quiz.q: A production database must remain fully operational and accepting writes for almost the entire migration process, with only a brief downtime window allowed at final cutover. What DMS capability enables this?
choices: A single one-time full load only
Full load followed by ongoing change data capture (CDC)
Manually pausing the database during migration
Migrating during a multi-day full outage
quiz.explain: CDC continuously captures and applies changes made after the initial full load, so only a short final sync is needed at cutover, minimizing downtime.

days.recap: DMS migrates data via full load plus optional ongoing CDC, homogeneous migrations (same engine) typically need only DMS, heterogeneous migrations (different engines) need SCT to convert schema and code first, and the full-load-plus-CDC pattern minimizes downtime by requiring only a brief final synchronization at cutover.

days.title: Modernizing Compute: Containers and Serverless

concepts.heading: Containerizing Monolithic Applications
concepts.body: Modernizing an existing monolithic EC2-based application often starts by containerizing it, packaging the application and its dependencies into a portable container image, then running that container on either Amazon ECS or Amazon EKS depending on the organization's existing orchestration expertise and portability requirements. Containerization alone, even before any deeper refactoring, typically improves deployment consistency, resource utilization, and horizontal scalability compared to running directly on dedicated EC2 instances.

concepts.heading: Choosing Between ECS and EKS
concepts.body: Amazon ECS is AWS's own container orchestration service, deeply integrated with other AWS services and generally considered simpler to operate for teams without existing Kubernetes expertise or requirements. Amazon EKS runs the standard, open-source Kubernetes control plane, which is the right choice when a team already has Kubernetes manifests, tooling, and operational experience they want to preserve, or when multi-cloud portability of the orchestration layer itself is a stated requirement. Both can run workloads on Fargate for serverless compute or on self-managed EC2 instances when more direct control over the underlying compute is needed.

concepts.heading: Serverless Modernization with Lambda and Step Functions
concepts.body: Workloads that run intermittently or in response to discrete events are strong candidates for modernizing directly to AWS Lambda, which eliminates idle compute cost entirely since billing is based only on actual invocation time, unlike an EC2 instance or container that incurs cost even while idle waiting for the next event. AWS Step Functions orchestrates complex, multi-step workflows composed of Lambda functions and other AWS service calls, handling retries, parallel execution branches, and state management natively, which removes the need to hand-write this coordination logic inside application code.

concepts.heading: Matching Modernization Approach to Workload Shape
concepts.body: The right modernization path depends on the workload's traffic shape and existing investment: steady, always-on, high-throughput workloads generally still favor containers (ECS or EKS) for cost-efficient sustained compute, intermittent or event-driven workloads favor Lambda to eliminate idle cost, and an organization with substantial existing Kubernetes tooling and expertise should weight that investment heavily toward EKS over ECS even where either would technically work.

examPoints: A scenario describing a need to preserve existing Kubernetes manifests and tooling while modernizing containers describes choosing Amazon EKS over ECS.
A scenario describing an intermittent batch workload that should incur no cost while idle describes modernizing to AWS Lambda.

quiz.q: A team modernizing its infrastructure already has substantial investment in Kubernetes manifests, tooling, and operational expertise, and wants to preserve that investment while moving to a managed AWS service. Which should they choose?
quiz.explain: EKS runs standard Kubernetes, preserving existing manifests and tooling; ECS (choice A) uses an AWS-native task and service model that would require rewriting that tooling.

quiz.q: A batch job runs unpredictably, sometimes several times a day and sometimes not for days, and the team wants to eliminate all idle compute cost. What modernization approach fits best?
choices: AWS Lambda, invoked only when the batch job needs to run
A large EKS cluster running at all times
Reserved Instances sized for peak load
quiz.explain: Lambda bills only for actual invocation time, eliminating idle cost for an unpredictable, intermittent workload; a continuously running instance or cluster (choices A and C) would incur cost even when idle.

days.recap: Containerization improves consistency and scalability over raw EC2, ECS suits AWS-native simplicity while EKS suits existing Kubernetes investment, Lambda eliminates idle cost for event-driven workloads with Step Functions orchestrating multi-step workflows, and the right choice depends on the workload's traffic shape and existing tooling investment.

days.title: Modernization Patterns: The Strangler Fig and Microservice Decomposition

concepts.heading: The Strangler Fig Pattern for Incremental Modernization
concepts.body: The strangler fig pattern modernizes a monolithic application incrementally rather than through a risky, all-at-once rewrite, by extracting new functionality (or a piece of existing functionality) into a new microservice while the rest of the application continues running unchanged, gradually shifting traffic for that piece to the new service. Over time, as more pieces are extracted, the surrounding legacy monolith shrinks (like a strangler fig gradually enveloping and eventually replacing its host tree), and by the time the monolith is fully replaced, the risk has been spread across many small, independently validated changes rather than concentrated in one large, high-risk cutover.

concepts.heading: API Gateway as a Routing Facade
concepts.body: Placing Amazon API Gateway in front of both the legacy monolith and any newly extracted microservices lets clients call a single, stable endpoint while the underlying implementation for any given route is free to change over time, from legacy monolith to new microservice, without the client ever needing to know. This facade pattern is what makes the strangler fig approach viable operationally, since the routing layer can be updated to redirect a specific path to the new service the moment it is ready, independent of when other paths are migrated.

concepts.heading: Decomposing Along Business Domain Boundaries
concepts.body: Effective microservice decomposition follows bounded contexts, natural business domain boundaries (such as separating order management from inventory management from customer accounts) rather than arbitrary technical boundaries, and typically gives each resulting microservice its own dedicated datastore instead of continuing to share one database across services. Sharing a database across microservices reintroduces tight coupling at the data layer even after the application code itself has been split apart, undermining much of the benefit of decomposition in the first place.

concepts.heading: Shifting to Event-Driven Communication
concepts.body: As services are decomposed, replacing direct synchronous calls between them with asynchronous, event-driven communication through EventBridge, SNS, or SQS further reduces coupling, since a service publishing an event does not need to know or care which other services are listening, and new consumers can be added later without changing the publisher at all. This event-driven shift is often layered on top of the strangler fig extraction itself, so newly extracted services are decoupled both from the legacy monolith and from each other from the moment they're created.

examPoints: A scenario describing incremental modernization of a monolith, extracting one piece of functionality at a time to limit risk, describes the strangler fig pattern.
A scenario describing a single stable client-facing endpoint that internally routes some paths to a legacy system and others to new microservices describes using API Gateway as a facade.

quiz.q: A company wants to modernize a large legacy monolith without the risk of a single, large rewrite-and-cutover event. Which pattern should it follow?
choices: A complete rewrite deployed all at once
The strangler fig pattern, extracting functionality incrementally
Shutting down the system during a full replacement
quiz.explain: The strangler fig pattern spreads risk across many small, incremental extractions rather than one large, high-risk cutover.

quiz.q: A team wants clients to keep calling a single stable API endpoint while some routes are served by a legacy monolith and others are gradually served by new microservices as they are built. What should sit in front of both?
choices: Direct client calls to each backend independently
Amazon API Gateway acting as a routing facade
No routing layer; clients choose the backend
A single Lambda function handling all logic
quiz.explain: API Gateway as a facade lets the routing for each path change independently and transparently to the client as functionality is migrated.

days.recap: The strangler fig pattern incrementally extracts functionality to limit modernization risk, API Gateway acts as a stable facade routing between legacy and new services, decomposition should follow business domain boundaries with per-service datastores, and shifting to event-driven communication (EventBridge/SNS/SQS) further reduces coupling between newly extracted services.

days.title: Domain 4 Review — Migration and Modernization

concepts.heading: Assessing Readiness Before Migrating
concepts.body: Domain 4 begins with assessment: AWS Transform maps on-premises server configuration and dependencies (replacing Application Discovery Service, closed to new customers since 2025-11-07), Migration Evaluator builds a data-driven cost projection for the business case, the 7 Rs framework (Retire, Retain, Rehost, Relocate, Repurchase, Replatform, Reengineer) categorizes the right approach per application, and AWS Transform also plans and tracks the migration once execution begins (Migration Hub, which did this before, has been closed to new customers since 2025-11-07).

concepts.heading: Moving Data and Servers
concepts.body: Data migration tools scale from AWS DataSync for online, ongoing transfer to AWS Data Transfer Terminal for offline transfer when bandwidth makes an online transfer impractical (Snow Family devices are no longer available to new customers), with Transfer Family preserving legacy SFTP/FTPS workflows. Server migration relies on AWS Application Migration Service (MGN) for continuous-replication, minimal-downtime rehosting, sharing its underlying technology with (but serving a different purpose from) AWS Elastic Disaster Recovery.

concepts.heading: Migrating Databases
concepts.body: Database migration pairs AWS DMS, which moves data via full load plus optional ongoing CDC, with the Schema Conversion Tool (SCT), which is required specifically for heterogeneous migrations between different database engines to convert schema and stored procedure code before DMS can move any data.

concepts.heading: Modernizing After Migration
concepts.body: Once workloads reach AWS, modernization moves them toward containers (ECS for AWS-native simplicity, EKS for existing Kubernetes investment) or serverless (Lambda for event-driven workloads, Step Functions for multi-step orchestration), matched to the workload's traffic shape and existing tooling.

concepts.heading: The Full SAP-C02 Arc
concepts.body: The four domains form one continuous arc for a Solutions Architect Professional: Domain 1 governs organizational complexity (accounts, networking, security, DR, cost) at the broadest scope, Domain 2 designs brand-new solutions with resilience and cost built in from day one, Domain 3 continuously improves already-running workloads across operations, security, performance, reliability, and cost, and Domain 4 evaluates, executes, and modernizes migrations bringing workloads onto that well-governed AWS foundation in the first place.

examPoints: When a Domain 4 scenario names a specific migration target (server, file data, or database), match it to its specific tool: servers to MGN, file data to DataSync or an offline transfer (AWS Data Transfer Terminal), and databases to DMS (plus SCT for heterogeneous engines).
The 7 Rs question type is reliably about matching a stated business constraint (speed, cost, cloud-native benefit) to the one R that best satisfies it, not about naming every R.

quiz.q: Which tool is required specifically when migrating between two different database engines with incompatible schema structures, before DMS can migrate any data?
quiz.explain: SCT converts schema and code for heterogeneous migrations; DMS alone cannot translate between fundamentally different database engines.

quiz.q: Which of the 7 Rs strategies involves rearchitecting an application to fully take advantage of cloud-native capabilities, typically requiring the most effort but capturing the most benefit?
quiz.explain: Reengineer/Refactor rearchitects the application for cloud-native capabilities, unlike Rehost, which moves it with minimal changes.

days.recap: Domain 4 wraps up: migration success depends on assessing readiness and dependencies first, choosing the right tool for each migration target (servers, files, databases), and modernizing to containers or serverless afterward, completing the full arc from organizational governance through new design, continuous improvement, and migration.

days.title: Final Practice Exam and Cross-Domain Review

concepts.heading: Simulating Exam Conditions
concepts.body: The final day should be spent taking one full-length, timed practice exam under conditions as close to the real SAP-C02 exam as possible: no notes, no interruptions, and the full allotted time, so that both knowledge gaps and pacing issues surface before the actual exam rather than during it. SAP-C02 scenarios are notably long and layered, often burying two or three distinct requirements inside one paragraph, so practicing the skill of reading quickly while still catching every stated constraint is as important as knowing the underlying services.

concepts.heading: Prioritizing the Most Important Constraint in a Scenario
concepts.body: When a scenario states multiple requirements at once, such as cost, availability, and security together, the correct answer is usually the option that best satisfies whichever constraint the question emphasizes most strongly (through words like 'must,' 'primary requirement,' or a specific numeric target), even if other answer choices would technically also work to a lesser degree. Practicing this triage skill, identifying the one non-negotiable constraint versus the nice-to-haves, on every remaining practice question is more valuable at this stage than reviewing any single service in isolation.

concepts.heading: Locking In Frequently Confused Service Pairs
concepts.body: A short, high-value final review targets the specific service pairs that are most commonly confused across all four domains: Transit Gateway versus PrivateLink, MGN versus DMS versus DataSync versus Snow Family, pilot light versus warm standby, Aurora Global Database versus DynamoDB Global Tables, and permission boundaries versus SCPs, among others. Writing a single distinguishing sentence for each pair, rather than re-reading full explanations, is the fastest way to make sure these distinctions are solid going into the exam.

concepts.heading: Reviewing by Domain Weight
concepts.body: With limited final review time, allocating attention roughly proportional to each domain's exam weight (Domain 2 at 29% and Domain 1 at 26% together make up more than half the exam, versus Domain 4 at 20%) ensures the highest-yield topics get the most attention rather than spreading review time evenly across all four domains regardless of their actual weight on the exam.

examPoints: In the final hours before the exam, prioritize resolving specific confused service pairs and reviewing by domain weight over learning any new material.
When a practice question presents a complex, multi-requirement scenario, practice explicitly identifying the single most emphasized constraint before evaluating the answer choices.

quiz.q: When a SAP-C02 scenario presents multiple requirements (cost, availability, and security) at once, what is the best strategy for selecting the correct answer?
choices: Identify which single requirement the scenario emphasizes most strongly and prioritize satisfying that one
Always choose the cheapest option regardless of other requirements
Always choose the most highly available option regardless of other requirements
quiz.explain: SAP-C02 scenarios typically have one dominant, emphasized constraint that determines the correct answer, even when multiple requirements are mentioned; defaulting to cost or availability alone (choices C and D) ignores what the specific scenario is actually emphasizing.

quiz.q: With limited time remaining before the exam, how should review time be allocated across the four domains?
choices: Equally across all four domains regardless of weight
Roughly proportional to each domain's exam weight, favoring Domains 1 and 2
Only on Domain 4, since it was studied most recently
Skip review entirely and rely on intuition
quiz.explain: Domains 1 and 2 together account for more than half the exam's weight, so proportionally weighting review time toward them yields the highest return on limited remaining study time.

days.recap: The 35-day plan concludes with a full timed practice exam, a strategy of prioritizing the most emphasized constraint in multi-requirement scenarios, targeted review of the most commonly confused service pairs, and final review time allocated by domain weight — completing preparation across all four SAP-C02 domains.
